Title: Pre-pour slab inspection
L1 Factual Knowledge: A pre-pour inspection checks important construction work before concrete placement makes that work difficult or impossible to inspect.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: The relevant work is inspected before the concrete pour and any identified issues are addressed before proceeding.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: The required checks depend on the work present at the stage and the applicable project requirements.
L4 Expert Judgement: An experienced practitioner looks for work that will become concealed by the concrete and therefore needs to be checked before the pour.
L5 Context and Dependencies: This activity depends on relevant pre-pour work being complete and occurs before concrete placement.

Title: Temporary wall frame bracing

L2 Procedural Knowledge: Bracing is installed as part of the framing sequence and remains in place while temporary stability is required.

L4 Expert Judgement: An experienced practitioner considers whether the partially completed frame can remain stable while subsequent work is carried out.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Temporary bracing is connected to the wall framing sequence and later stability of the structure.

Title: Stud Spacing Selection — Wet Area vs Standard Wall
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00001: Stud Spacing Selection — Wet Area vs Standard Wall. Trigger: Carpenter begins pricing or setting out wall frames and must determine the correct stud spacing for each wall type.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Drawings (or verbal brief) are received and the wall type/use is known. Wet area designation is either shown on the plan or confirmed with the builder. Selection rule: Use 450 mm centres in any wet area — this is non-negotiable and the practitioner described it as 'end of story'. Use 600 mm centres in non-loadbearing standard walls. Use wider stud section (120–140 mm) where the required insulation R-value cannot be accommodated within a 90 mm stud. For loadbearing walls, consult AS 1684.2 for applicable spacing.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Wet area status (changes spacing regardless of loading); wall height (2.4 m, 2.7 m, 3.0 m — affects bracing but not stud size); wind zone (affects bracing calculation); insulation R-value required; loadbearing vs non-loadbearing classification. Alternatives: 450 mm stud centres (wet area); 600 mm stud centres (standard wall); 120/140 mm stud section where high-R insulation is required.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Incorrect stud spacing in wet area — 600 mm used instead of 450 mm. Consequence: Wrong spacing installed → lining not adequately supported → tile movement and cracking → water ingress at tile joints → substrate saturation → mould, structural damage → warranty claim. Time to visible: 6–24 months. Cost to rectify: tile removal, reframing, waterproof, retile.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Framing inspection by certifier confirms stud spacing is correct before lining proceeds. Visual check against plan-specified wet area designation. Concealment point: Lining conceals stud spacing after plasterboard is fixed. No access to frame after this point without demolition. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Roof Geometry Set-Out Sequence — Mark Roof Before Erecting Walls
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00002: Roof Geometry Set-Out Sequence — Mark Roof Before Erecting Walls. Trigger: Carpenter begins assembling wall frames and must determine the order of set-out operations before erection.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Top and bottom wall plates are laid out flat on the ground. Drawings are available and have been reviewed. Roof type and geometry are known. Selection rule: Mark the roof set-out (jack rafter position, half-span, first common rafter centre) on the wall plates while they are flat on the ground. This is significantly safer and more accurate than doing the same work from a ladder after the frame is erected. The set-out also determines where studs must be positioned to maintain the continuous load path from roof to slab.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Roof type (hip, gable, skillion — changes the set-out geometry); roof sheet type (1200 mm vs 900 mm rafter/purlin centres for sheet metal); building span; architect specification of rafter spacing; number of storeys. Alternatives: Mark roof set-out on the plates while they are flat on the ground (preferred); mark roof set-out after walls are erected (from a ladder).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Roof set-out done from a ladder after erection — increased error rate, safety risk, and time cost. Or studs positioned first without regard to roof load paths. Consequence: Error in set-out → rafter positions misaligned with studs → load path discontinuity → double top plate or blocking required as a corrective measure (adds cost and time) → OR roof geometry errors require truss/rafter relocation before lining. Safety risk: working at height to correct what could have been done safely at ground level.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Roof set-out marks are visible on the top plate. Rafter/truss positions align with stud positions below, confirming load path continuity. Certifier framing inspection. Concealment point: Roof geometry is effectively locked in once rafters/trusses are installed and the roof frame is permanent-braced. No opportunity to revise the geometry after this point without significant rework. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Double Top Plate or Blocking — When Load Path Continuity Requires It
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00003: Double Top Plate or Blocking — When Load Path Continuity Requires It. Trigger: Carpenter discovers or anticipates that a roof member (rafter or truss) will not bear directly over a stud below, breaking the continuous load path.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Wall plates are set out (or being set out). The roof member positions are known from the set-out marks or truss layout. A misalignment between roof member and stud is identified. Selection rule: Where a roof member loads the top plate at a point that does not bear directly over a stud, a double top plate or blocking must be provided to distribute that load to the nearest stud. The double plate acts as a transfer element. Blocking is an alternative where space permits. The preferred approach — identified by the practitioner — is to mark roo
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Degree of misalignment between rafter/truss and stud (small misalignment may be acceptable under AS 1684.2; larger requires intervention); whether trusses or cut rafters are used (trusses are manufactured to a layout that may not align with studs); presence of girder trusses (concentrated loads at specific points); wall height and span. Alternatives: Install a double top plate to transfer load across to the nearest stud; install blocking between studs at the point of load application; redesign the set-out to realign roof member
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Load path discontinuity not addressed — no double plate or blocking installed where required. Consequence: Concentrated roof load applied to top plate at a point with no stud below → top plate deflection over time → ceiling and wall cracking → in severe cases, structural movement visible in frame → engineer assessment required → costly remediation involving lining removal and structural intervention.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Visual inspection: the double plate or blocking is visible during the framing inspection. Certifier framing hold point confirms load path is continuous before lining. Concealment point: Once lining is fixed, the load transfer arrangement is permanently concealed. No access without strip-out. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Temporary Bracing of Erected Wall Frames
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00004: Temporary Bracing of Erected Wall Frames. Trigger: A wall frame has been stood upright and must be stabilised before workers can proceed on or around it and before permanent bracing is installed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Wall frame is erected (plumbed and squared). Slab is available for bracing anchor fixings. The location of any in-slab services is known (or must be confirmed before drilling). Selection rule: Every wall frame must be temporarily braced immediately after erection and before any person works on or around it. The frame acts like a sail under wind load and is structurally unstable until permanent bracing is complete. Temporary bracing is fixed to the slab — either with masonry nails or masonry anchors. Anchors are preferred where in-slab serv
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Wind exposure at the time of construction (higher wind = more bracing required); presence and location of in-slab services (changes fixing method); height and length of wall frame; temporary loads from workers; time between erection and permanent bracing installation. Alternatives: Ply sheet bracing fixed to the face of the wall; Speedbrace / steel diagonal brace; combination of face and diagonal bracing; number and spacing of braces determined by wind exposure and frame dimensions.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No temporary bracing installed after wall erection, or bracing is inadequate for the wind/load conditions. Consequence: Unbraced wall frame in wind → frame acts as a sail → frame overturns or racks → potential collapse of frame onto workers below or adjacent → injury or fatality. Even partial racking before collapse: frame geometry distorted → permanent bracing installed to a twisted frame → plumb/square problems carry through to lining and finishes. Immediate risk: High.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Frame is plumb (checked with spirit level or plumb bob) and square (diagonals checked). Bracing is fixed at both face and slab. Certifier framing inspection will check permanent bracing — temporary bracing is removed before this point. Concealment point: Temporary bracing is removed before permanent bracing inspection. There is no long-term concealment risk for temporary bracing itself, but inadequate bracing during the construction phase creates an immediate collapse risk. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021 + WHS Regulations SA;

Title: Provisional Sum for Unquantifiable Subgrade or Site Unknowns
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00005: Provisional Sum for Unquantifiable Subgrade or Site Unknowns. Trigger: Builder is pricing a project and encounters a scope item — typically subgrade works, demolition, or excavation — where the quantity or condition cannot be confirmed before construction commences.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Builder has reviewed the drawings and conducted a site investigation. One or more scope items cannot be quantified reliably from surface information alone (e.g. buried roots, unknown fill, uncertain soil depth). Selection rule: Where a scope item cannot be reasonably quantified before construction, identify it as a provisional sum in the contract scope letter. Document the uncertainty clearly. When the item is encountered and its actual extent is established, claim the actual cost with supporting evidence. This protects both the builder (f
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Nature and extent of the uncertainty (known vs unknown unknowns); whether the soil report provides relevant information; client relationship and contract type; project stage at which the uncertainty is encountered; whether the item can be deferred until after initial excavation reveals the condition. Alternatives: Include the uncertain item as a fixed-price allowance (risk carried by the builder); exclude the item entirely and advise the client separately; identify the item as a provisional sum in the contract — a claimable item
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Uncertain item priced as a fixed sum — builder carries the full risk of the unknown condition. Consequence: Unknown item exceeds the fixed-price allowance → builder absorbs cost overrun → disputes with client → project delay while additional scope is negotiated → in worst case, builder financially exposed on a large unquantified risk. Alternatively: item excluded, client is surprised by an additional cost after contract is signed → relationship breakdown.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: When the provisional item is encountered during construction, the builder documents the actual condition with photographs and a written record before remediation. Variation/provisional sum claim is submitted with this evidence. Concealment point: Once excavation is backfilled and slab is poured, the subgrade condition that justified the provisional sum claim is no longer visible. Documentation before remediation is essential. Standard reference: None — commercial/contractual; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/

Title: Builder Two-Stage Verification — Independent Check Despite Licensed Trade
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00006: Builder Two-Stage Verification — Independent Check Despite Licensed Trade. Trigger: A licensed trade completes or is about to complete a stage of work that will be concealed or that carries sign-off liability for the building supervisor.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Work has been (or is about to be) completed by a licensed trade. The building supervisor holds sign-off responsibility for the stage. The work is about to be concealed (lining, slab, render) or inspected by a certifier. Selection rule: The building supervisor must independently verify the work of every licensed trade before sign-off, regardless of the trade's licence status. The licence establishes minimum competence but does not transfer the supervisor's sign-off responsibility. 'I don't trust any trade — they're the licensed trade, but I
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Stage of work (higher risk at concealment points — under-slab plumbing, framing before lining); trade experience and track record on this project; hold-point requirements from the certifier; time and programme pressure (common cause of skipped verification). Alternatives: Accept the licensed trade's work without independent inspection (rely solely on their licence and professional responsibility); independently verify the work before sign-off even though the trade is licensed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Supervisor accepts licensed trade's work without independent verification. Trade has made an error — incorrect pipe position, missing structural fixing, incorrect material specification. Consequence: Undetected error concealed by the next stage → error discovered after occupation, after sale, or at warranty claim → building supervisor is liable as the sign-off authority → investigation reveals no documented independent check was made → professional indemnity claim, licence risk, legal exposure. The concealment of defective work by a subsequ
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Supervisor's independent inspection is documented — photographs, checklist, or written note — before the work is concealed or signed off. Hold-point documentation from certifier where required. Concealment point: Once work is concealed (slab poured, lining fixed, render applied), independent verification is no longer possible without destructive investigation. Standard reference: Building Work Contractors Act 1995 (SA) + WHS Act 2012 (SA); clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Starte

Title: Hydrostatic Test and OTR Inspection Protocol — Under-Slab Sanitary Drainage
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00007: Hydrostatic Test and OTR Inspection Protocol — Under-Slab Sanitary Drainage. Trigger: Under-slab sanitary drainage is complete and must be inspected and tested before the slab is poured.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: All under-slab drainage, lagging, bedding, supports and brackets are installed. Certificate of Compliance (COC) and as-constructed drawing are prepared. Inspection is booked with the Office of the Technical Regulator (OTR) before 3:00 pm on the day prior to the intended test. Selection rule: Book the OTR inspection before 3pm on the day prior. Ensure the drain remains completely exposed and unbackfilled — the inspector must see all elements. Place the system under hydrostatic test at 10 kPa minimum for a minimum of 15 minutes before the in
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Weather forecast (rain can destroy bedding before inspection); site programme and scheduling pressure; proximity of the slab pour date; quality of bedding installation; risk of drain settlement on filled sites. Alternatives: Book inspection and test on schedule; postpone inspection if bedding/installation is not ready; book inspection knowing it may not be attended (volume-builder strategy — not recommended).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Drain not tested before slab pour; drain not compliant with grade or bedding requirements; inspection not booked; COC not lodged. Consequence: Defect concealed under slab → settlement causes low point in drain → blockage and gurgling at floor wastes (first symptom: anti-siphonage failure) → camera investigation required → slab cutting to expose and replace drain section → loss of building use during works → cost: $5,000–$30,000+ depending on extent. Plumber's licence number on COC means 5-year personal liability exposure.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: OTR inspector issues approval (or no-objection notice). COC is lodged. Slab pour can proceed. All documentation retained by the plumber for the 5-year compliance window. Concealment point: Once the slab is poured, the under-slab drainage is permanently concealed. Any defect discovered after the slab is poured requires core-drilling or slab saw-cutting to investigate and rectify — extremely costly. Camera inspection can be used but is expensive and not always conclusive. Standard reference: WHS Act 2012 (SA) s.84-85; clause verific

Title: Under-Slab vs External Sanitary Drain Routing
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00008: Under-Slab vs External Sanitary Drain Routing. Trigger: Plumber is assessing the drainage design for a new dwelling and must determine whether the sanitary drain will run beneath the slab or externally along the outside of the building.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Site is visited. Drawings and site plan are available. The depth of the sewer connection to the street has been confirmed. The site layout and available side-access space is assessed. Selection rule: Check the depth of the sewer connection first — this is the controlling datum. If sufficient external side space exists (typically at least 1.5–2 m given the 300 mm cover requirement and the height-to-length geometry as the drain descends below the footings), an external route is feasible. If the side space is insufficient — as is common on ti
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Width of available side space; depth of the sewer connection (the deeper the connection, the more fall is available before the drain descends below footing level); footing type and depth; site slope; whether the drain must pass through or under footing beams (requiring lagging); presence of stormwater pipes competing for side-access space. Alternatives: Run the sanitary drain externally around the outside of the building; run the sanitary drain beneath the slab.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: External route attempted on a site where the geometry does not support it — drain cannot maintain minimum cover and required gradient simultaneously. Or under-slab drain installed without adequate bedding or expansion control. Consequence: External route failure: drain runs too shallow (< 300 mm) — vulnerable to garden spikes and root intrusion → pipe breakage → sewage in garden. Under-slab failure: inadequate bedding → settlement under slab → cracked pipe → effluent in fill beneath slab → slab heave or structural movement → very expensive
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Under-slab route: drain is inspected and hydrostatic tested before slab pour (see CDO-00007). External route: drain is inspected and tested before backfilling. Grade is checked with a level. Concealment point: Under-slab: permanently concealed by the slab once poured. External route: concealed once backfilled and paths/landscaping are installed. Standard reference: Safe Work Australia Plant Code + WHS Regulations SA; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: SWMS vs Take 5 — Hazard Documentation and Escalation Selection
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00009: SWMS vs Take 5 — Hazard Documentation and Escalation Selection. Trigger: A worker or supervisor observes or is notified of a WHS hazard during the course of work.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: A responsible WHS person is designated for the site. Workers have access to Take 5 materials. Site SWMS is in place. Selection rule: Use Take 5 for isolated, immediately manageable hazards; SWMS for complex or systemic issues. Urgency, complexity, and number of workers affected determine the escalation level.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Medium Alternatives: Use a Take 5 for a simple, immediate, manageable hazard — quick record, immediate action, add to SWMS if needed. Escalate to the full SWMS process where the hazard is complex, involves multiple workers, or requires a formal procedural response. Call a toolbox meeting where the hazard affects the programme for the day or multiple trades.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Undocumented hazard persists → same or different worker injured → no record to show the hazard was identified and managed → site/builder liable for failure to document and control → WHS prosecution risk. If the hazard leads to a fatality, the absence of documentation is a significant aggravating factor. Consequence: Difficult — if injury has occurred from an undocumented hazard, the legal and reputational consequences cannot be reversed. The documentation failure compounds the original safety failure.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Some hazards — particularly in confined or concealed locations — may be concealed by subsequent work if not addressed promptly. Concealment point: Hazard not documented — no Take 5 or SWMS entry made. Hazard continues to exist. Worker or visitor subsequently injured. Standard reference: Safe Work Australia Asbestos Code + Environment Protection Act 1993 (SA); clause verification: not recorded. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/.

Title: Site Induction — Universal Requirement Before Entry
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00010: Site Induction — Universal Requirement Before Entry. Trigger: Any person — worker, subcontractor, inspector, visitor — approaches the site boundary to enter for the first time or after conditions have materially changed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Site is operational and has workers, hazards, or plant present. A person intends to enter the site. Selection rule: Every person entering the site — regardless of experience, White Card status, trade licence, or number of previous site visits — receives a site-specific induction before entry. Even repeat subcontractors on annual or periodic induction cycles receive an update when site conditions have materially changed. Inspectors, bank representatives, and union officials are not exempt. White Card provides baseline awareness but does not
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Frequency of visits by the same person (annual induction vs every visit); whether site conditions have changed since the last induction; type of visitor (worker, inspector, owner); current site hazards. Alternatives: Provide site-specific induction before entry; allow entry without induction on the basis that the person is experienced/has a White Card.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Person enters site without induction. Site conditions, plant movements, or hazards differ from their expectation. Person is injured or causes injury to others. Consequence: Uninducted person encounters a site-specific hazard → injury → investigation reveals no induction record → builder/PCBU liable for failure to provide site-specific induction → WHS prosecution or civil liability. The absence of an induction record is often the decisive factor in liability determinations.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Induction record is signed by the entrant. Site register shows all current personnel have been inducted. Emergency contact and evacuation point are confirmed understood. Concealment point: There is no concealment point for an induction failure — but the consequence of a person entering without site-specific knowledge is that they act on general assumptions rather than actual current site conditions. Standard reference: WHS Act 2012 (SA) s.17; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Sta

Title: Worker Override Authority — Safety-First Escalation Despite Supervisor
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00011: Worker Override Authority — Safety-First Escalation Despite Supervisor. Trigger: A worker identifies a condition they consider critical or seriously hazardous. The site supervisor has assessed it differently — as manageable or non-critical.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Work is underway. A hazard is identified. There is a disagreement between the worker and the supervisor about the level of risk. The worker has a genuine belief that the hazard presents a serious risk. Selection rule: Where a worker genuinely believes a hazard presents a serious risk, they have the right and responsibility to escalate that assessment even when the supervisor does not share it. A gas leak that is described as 'only a little bit' is still a gas leak — a small leak can still cause health effects without ignition. The selectio
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Nature and immediacy of the hazard; relative expertise of the worker and supervisor; programme pressure; whether other workers are at risk; regulatory requirements. Alternatives: Accept the supervisor's assessment and continue work; escalate the hazard as critical and stop work if necessary regardless of the supervisor's view.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Worker defers to the supervisor and continues work in the presence of a genuinely serious hazard. Hazard materialises. Consequence: Gas leak normalised → accumulation → ignition or health effects → workers injured or fatality → investigation reveals worker raised concern and was overridden → supervisor and PCBU liable → workers' compensation and WHS prosecution.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: The hazard is resolved — either by demonstrating it is genuinely non-critical, or by stopping work and remedying the condition. The resolution is documented in the Take 5 or SWMS. Concealment point: Some hazards — gas accumulation, structural instability — become harder to assess as conditions change. The window for safe intervention may close. Standard reference: Safe Work Australia Welding Code + AS 2444:2001; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Plant and Pedestrian Separation — Active Control at Site Interface
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00012: Plant and Pedestrian Separation — Active Control at Site Interface. Trigger: Plant (bobcat, excavator, crane, concrete truck) is operating on or moving through a site where workers or public pedestrians are present or may be present.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Plant operation is planned or underway. Non-essential workers are cleared from the operating zone. If the plant must cross a public footpath, a second person is designated as a spotter. Selection rule: During plant clearing, excavation or material delivery, no non-essential person is in the operating zone. This is non-negotiable — rely on exclusion, not operator awareness. Where plant must cross a public footpath, a dedicated second person controls the sequence — pedestrians stop before plant moves, or plant stops for pedestrians. Simultan
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Type of plant (bobcat vs semi-trailer); proximity to public footpath; pedestrian volume; site boundary position; council permissions; visibility conditions. Alternatives: Rely on the plant operator's awareness alone; use a dedicated spotter/traffic controller; obtain formal council permission to divert pedestrians; prevent simultaneous plant and pedestrian movement.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Plant and pedestrians share a space without active separation. Operator does not see a pedestrian. Collision occurs. Consequence: Plant-pedestrian collision → serious injury or fatality → investigation reveals no dedicated spotter, no formal separation → PCBU and site supervisor liable → WHS prosecution, civil liability, reputational damage.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: The operating zone is clear of non-essential personnel. A spotter is in position before plant moves to or across the site boundary. No pedestrian-plant conflict occurs. Concealment point: Plant movements on site create an immediate risk that is not concealed — but the consequences of a collision are severe and irreversible. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3000:2018 (Wiring Rules) + SA Electricity Act + WHS Regulations SA; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Hazardous Discovery During Excavation — Stop Work and Specialist Response
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00013: Hazardous Discovery During Excavation — Stop Work and Specialist Response. Trigger: Excavation or trenching work encounters an unexpected material — pipe, container, waste, or material that may be hazardous.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Excavation is underway. A material is struck that was not anticipated in the site investigation. Its identity and hazard level are uncertain. Selection rule: Stop work immediately when an unexpected material is encountered and its hazard level cannot be confirmed from visual inspection. Do not attempt to establish the extent of the material by further excavation. Where asbestos is confirmed or suspected, notify the EPA and engage a licensed asbestos removalist before any further disturbance. Where the material is non-hazardous (confirmed b
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Site history and likely materials; type and condition of the material; whether further disturbance has occurred before the hazard was recognised; regulatory requirements for the specific material type. Alternatives: Continue excavation to establish extent; stop work immediately and bring in a specialist; stop work, establish a cordon, and notify authorities (where the material is or may be asbestos or other regulated hazardous substance).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Excavation continues after hazardous material is struck. Material is fragmented and dispersed. Workers are exposed to fibres or contaminants. Consequence: Asbestos pipe struck and fragmented → fibres released → workers and neighbours exposed → stop-work order from EPA → specialist remediation required → civil liability for exposure → regulatory prosecution. Old-farm sites with buried asbestos cement pipe are a specific risk on greenfield SA residential sites.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Work is stopped. A cordon is established. The specialist or authority is notified. No further disturbance occurs until the material is assessed. Documentation of the discovery, response, and clearance is retained. Concealment point: Once hazardous material is disturbed — particularly asbestos — fibres are released and cannot be recalled. Further disturbance dramatically increases exposure risk and remediation cost. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3:2018; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Sta

Title: End-of-Project WHS Review — Incident Pattern Analysis
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00014: End-of-Project WHS Review — Incident Pattern Analysis. Trigger: A construction project reaches practical completion. Safety records, Take 5s, toolbox meeting notes, and incident reports have been accumulated across the project duration.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Project is at or near completion. WHS documentation from the project is available. The builder or WHS manager has time to conduct a review before the project is closed out. Selection rule: At project completion, review all WHS records — Take 5s, toolbox notes, incidents — and assess whether any incidents or near-misses are part of a pattern. Where the same type of incident has occurred more than once, investigate whether it reflects a systemic issue (task design, site condition, training gap, management failure) rather than individual erro
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Number and type of incidents; whether incidents are isolated or form a pattern; whether the pattern has been seen on previous projects; available corrective measures. Alternatives: File the documentation and close out the project without review; conduct a project-level review of incidents and near-misses; conduct a longitudinal review across multiple projects to identify recurring patterns.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No end-of-project review is conducted. A hazard pattern that caused multiple incidents on this project is not identified. The same pattern causes a more serious incident on the next project. Consequence: Recurring hazard unidentified → same incident occurs on next project but more severely → investigation asks whether the pattern was known → no review record → builder/PCBU liable for failure to learn from prior incidents → potential gross negligence finding where the pattern was observable.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Review is documented. Patterns are identified or confirmed absent. Corrective measures are recorded and assigned. Findings are transferred to the next project's WHS planning. Concealment point: No concealment risk — the review process is administrative. source_content.l1: Decision captured in CDO-00014: End-of-Project WHS Review — Incident Pattern Analysis. Trigger: A construction project reaches practical completion. Safety records, Take 5s, toolbox meeting notes, and incident reports have been accumulated across the project duration.
source_content.l2: Preconditions: Project is at or near completion. WHS documentation from the project is available. The builder or WHS manager has time to conduct a review before the project is closed out. Selection rule: At project completion, review all WHS records — Take 5s, toolbox notes, incidents — and assess whether any incidents or near-misses are part of a pattern. source_content.l3: Conditions and variables: Number and type of incidents; whether incidents are isolated or form a pattern; whether the pattern has been seen on previous projects; available corrective measures. Alternatives: File the documentation and close out the project without review; conduct a project-level review of incidents and near-misses; conduct a longitudinal review across multiple projects to identify recurring patterns.
source_content.l4: Failure mode: No end-of-project review is conducted. A hazard pattern that caused multiple incidents on this project is not identified. The same pattern causes a more serious incident on the next project. Consequence: Recurring hazard unidentified → same incident occurs on next project but more severely → investigation asks whether the pattern was known → no review record → builder/PCBU liable for failure to learn from prior incidents → potential gross negligence finding where the pattern was observable.

Title: Hot Work Near Combustibles — Fire Control and Trade Coordination
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00015: Hot Work Near Combustibles — Fire Control and Trade Coordination. Trigger: A trade performing hot work (soldering, welding, angle grinding) is about to work in proximity to combustible materials — paint, timber, roofing material, insulation.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Hot work is planned. Combustible materials are present in the work zone or adjacent area. Other trades may be working in the same space. Selection rule: Before any hot work begins, confirm: (1) appropriate fire extinguishers are present on site — both water (for timber/materials) and dry chemical (for flammable liquids/electrical); (2) other trades are not working simultaneously with combustible materials in the same space; (3) a fire watch is maintained during and immediately after hot work. A painter applying solvent-based coatings and a
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Type of hot work; type of combustible material; enclosure/ventilation; proximity of other trades; weather/wind conditions. Alternatives: Conduct hot work without fire controls; require a hot work permit and fire watch; resequence trades to separate hot work from combustible operations.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Hot work proceeds while other trades are using combustible coatings or materials in the same space. Ignition occurs. Consequence: Plumber soldering near painter using solvent-based undercoat → paint ignites → fire spreads → damage to structure, tools, materials → possible injury → investigation reveals concurrent trades in the same space → site supervisor liable for failure to coordinate hot work with combustible operations.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Fire extinguishers are confirmed present and appropriate before hot work begins. No other trades with combustible materials are working in the immediate zone. Fire watch is maintained. No ignition occurs. Concealment point: Once combustible material ignites, the window for effective intervention is very short — particularly in enclosed or partially enclosed buildings. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3:2018; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Electrical Isolation and Tag-Off Before Live Circuit Work
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00016: Electrical Isolation and Tag-Off Before Live Circuit Work. Trigger: Any person is about to work on, near, or with electrical equipment or circuits — including painters removing power-point covers, plumbers testing near hot-water services, or a second trade entering a space where electrical work is underway.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Electrical work has been commenced or completed to a stage where circuits may be live or partially connected. Another trade or visitor is about to enter the same space or interact with electrical elements. Selection rule: Before any trade works on or near an electrical circuit — and before any meter or connection is made live — the circuit must be confirmed isolated and tagged off. A tag is a physical and visible lock that prevents the circuit from being energised by another person. The painter who turned the power on while the electrician
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Stage of electrical installation (rough-in vs final fix vs connected); number and variety of trades in the space; programme pressure; whether the meter has been connected by the network provider. Alternatives: Work proceeds on the assumption that the circuit is de-energised; apply isolation and tag-off before any electrical work or related trade work near electrical elements.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Tag-off is not applied or is removed by a person other than the one who applied it. A circuit is energised while another person is working on or near it. Consequence: Energised circuit → electrocution or arc flash → serious injury or fatality → investigation reveals no tag applied or tag removed by wrong person → licensed electrician and PCBU liable → WHS prosecution → potential manslaughter charge if gross negligence is found.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Tag is visibly applied to the isolation point. No circuit is energised without the knowledge and consent of the person who applied the tag. Electrical work is completed and signed off before any related trade is allowed to proceed in the same space. Concealment point: Once a circuit is live, its hazard is invisible — energised conductors look identical to de-energised ones. The concealment is inherent in the nature of electricity. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3:2018 + Manufacturer technical data; clause verification: Verified.

Title: Roof Catchment Sizing — ARI Selection and Effective Area Calculation
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00017: Roof Catchment Sizing — ARI Selection and Effective Area Calculation. Trigger: A roof plumber receives plans for a new dwelling and must size the roof drainage system — gutters, downpipes, and overflow provision.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Plans and specifications are available. Project location is confirmed. Roof pitch is stated on the plan. Selection rule: Identify the project location and look up the 20-year ARI rainfall intensity for that location. Convert the 2D plan area to effective sloping catchment area using the pitch multiplier. Divide the roof into drainage zones, each with one or more downpipes. For each zone, calculate the peak flow rate in litres per second and confirm that the selected gutter profile and downpipe diameter can pass that flow. Where software is
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Geographic location (changes ARI intensity); roof pitch (changes effective catchment area); roof type and profile (changes available gutter/downpipe options); building form (broken hips, valleys, porticos increase complexity); design event (20-year ARI for domestic, other for commercial). Alternatives: Manual calculation using standards tables and pitch multipliers; sizing software (e.g. Lysaght, manufacturer tools) with manual verification; accept the drawn specification without checking.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Drainage system sized below the design event. Gutters overflow in a significant rainfall. Water enters the building or causes damage. Consequence: Under-sized gutter overflows in a design event → water runs behind cladding or through ceiling penetrations → ceiling damage, mould, structural damage → warranty claim → investigation finds drainage was under-sized relative to the applicable ARI → roof plumber liable for design/sizing failure. Climate-change note: design events may occur more frequently than the ARI interval implies.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Calculation is documented and matches the installed gutter, downpipe, and overflow configuration. Where software is used, manual cross-check of one zone is retained as evidence of verification. Concealment point: Once gutters, downpipes, and roof sheets are installed and ceilings are lined, the drainage system is effectively locked in. No visible indication of under-sizing until a significant rainfall event. Standard reference: WHS Act 2012 (SA) s.17 — general duty of care; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C:

Title: Overflow Provision — Deliberate Design for Extreme Rainfall
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00018: Overflow Provision — Deliberate Design for Extreme Rainfall. Trigger: A roof drainage system is being designed. Normal capacity has been sized for the 20-year ARI. A decision must be made about how the system behaves in a rainfall event that exceeds this capacity.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Normal gutter and downpipe capacity is established. The building form and surroundings are known. The overflow path and any architectural features that may obstruct it are identified. Selection rule: A deliberate overflow path must be provided as part of the gutter design — not as an optional extra. Freeboard provides some buffer, but the standard requires overflow to be managed, not merely tolerated. For standard domestic gutters (D or OG profile), a controlled back overflow arrangement is a common acceptable method. For box gutters, a de
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Gutter profile (determines what overflow methods are available); building form (parapet, box gutter, balcony — each requires different treatment); architectural covers/shrouds on rainheads; proximity of the overflow path to habitable areas or neighbouring property. Alternatives: Controlled back overflow (gutter set off the fascia so extreme water overflows away from the building); rainhead with overflow slot; sump/slot overflow; reliance on freeboard alone without a deliberate overflow path.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No deliberate overflow path provided. Extreme rainfall event exceeds gutter capacity. Water overflows into the building rather than away from it. Consequence: No overflow provision → extreme rainfall → water backs up behind fascia or flows into roof space → ceiling damage, mould, structural damage to top plates → warranty claim → investigation finds no overflow provision → builder and roof plumber liable.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: The overflow path is traceable from the design drawings. Where a controlled back overflow is used, the gutter is set off the fascia at the correct distance. Where a rainhead is used, the overflow geometry is unobstructed. The overflow discharges to a location that does not damage the building or neighbouring property. Concealment point: Once the roof and cladding are complete, the overflow arrangement is concealed or inaccessible. Failure is only discovered during a significant rainfall event. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3:201

Title: Gutter Fall Management — Long Runs and Visual Alignment
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00019: Gutter Fall Management — Long Runs and Visual Alignment. Trigger: A long gutter run must be set out and brackets fixed. The gutter must drain correctly while also reading cleanly on the facade.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Run length is measured. Fascia depth is confirmed. Downpipe positions are provisionally established. Minimum fall is known from the applicable standard. Selection rule: For long gutter runs, a single continuous fall from one end to the other will exhaust the available fascia depth before the required fall is achieved — the high end sits at the top of the fascia and the low end sits at the bottom, which looks wrong and limits overflow freeboard. Instead, divide the run by introducing a high point near the midpoint and falling in both direct
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Total run length; fascia depth; minimum fall (typically 1:500 or as specified); number and position of downpipes; aesthetic requirements; whether additional downpipes can be added. Alternatives: Single fall from one end to the other; mid-point high point falling to both ends; multiple subtle high points creating a zig-zag fall pattern with multiple downpipes.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Single continuous fall on a long run exhausts the fascia depth. Gutter looks noticeably sloped, or minimum fall is not achieved at the high end. Consequence: Inadequate fall → water sits in the low sections of the gutter → debris and sediment accumulate → gutter blocks → overflow at the low point → water behind fascia → fascia and rafter-end rot.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Gutter reads cleanly on the facade without visible slope. Each section of gutter meets minimum fall. All downpipes are within capacity. Gutter holds bracket alignment without visible sag. Concealment point: Once cladding is complete and scaffolding is removed, gutter fall errors are only discovered by inspection or when drainage fails. Re-fixing gutter fall after cladding is complete is difficult without damaging finished surfaces. Standard reference: NCC 2022 Vol 2, Part H5 + SA Development Regulations 2008; clause verification:

Title: Valley Sheet Fixing — Thermal Movement Allowance
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00020: Valley Sheet Fixing — Thermal Movement Allowance. Trigger: A valley is being installed over a roof junction. The fixing method must be selected.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Valley sheet material and dimensions are known. Roof pitch and orientation are known. Thermal conditions at the location are assessed (extreme temperature range). Selection rule: Valley sheets are flat — unlike corrugated roof sheeting, they have no profile geometry to absorb thermal movement. On a hot day, a flat metal valley sheet will expand along its length. If it is screw-fixed in a way that restrains that movement, the sheet will tear around the fixing over time. The correct fixing method allows the sheet to slide while remaining wea
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Material type (different metals have different thermal expansion coefficients); valley length (longer valleys experience greater total movement); local temperature range; roof orientation and shading. Alternatives: Traditional folded/held fixing that allows movement; direct screw fixing that restrains the sheet.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Valley sheet screw-fixed in a restraining manner. Sheet expands and contracts with temperature changes. Sheet tears around fixings over several seasons. Consequence: Fixing failure → hole in valley sheet → water enters roof space → ceiling damage, mould, potential structural damage → warranty claim or defect liability → concealed by overlapping sheets, difficult to diagnose without destructive investigation.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Fixing method is consistent with the applicable standard or manufacturer requirement. No rigid fixings restrain thermal movement along the length of the sheet. Concealment point: Valley sheets are concealed by the overlapping roof sheets from above. Once installed, the fixing method is not visible. Failure (tearing around fixings) appears as a water leak, often years after installation. Standard reference: Building Work Contractors Act 1995 (SA) + applicable AS (decision-specific); clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes

Title: Roof Sheet Corrosion — Prevention of Trade-Created Damage from Grinder Sparks
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00021: Roof Sheet Corrosion — Prevention of Trade-Created Damage from Grinder Sparks. Trigger: A following trade — typically an electrician, HVAC installer, or another post-roofing contractor — needs to make a penetration through or near the installed roof sheeting.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Roof sheeting is installed and its protective coating is intact. The following trade is about to begin work that involves a grinder or angle grinder. Selection rule: Hot metal filings from a grinder landing on coated roof sheeting will burn through the protective coating at the point of contact. The coating damage is small but sufficient to initiate corrosion, which then spreads beneath the surface. The damage may not be immediately visible, but within months the affected spots will rust visibly. A $25,000 roof can be compromised by a sing
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Coating type and hardness (more important for pre-painted steel than unpainted materials); proximity of the grinding operation to the finished sheets; wind direction (determines where sparks travel); whether the work can be done off the roof. Alternatives: Use a grinder directly on or over the finished roof sheeting; use a drill, nibbler, or tin snips that do not produce sparks; make penetrations in the workshop/on the ground before installation; relocate the work so grinding does not occur over finished sheets.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Grinder is used over the finished roof without a briefing or protection. Sparks land on the coating. Corrosion initiates. Consequence: Coating damage → corrosion → visible rust patches within 6-18 months → warranty claim → investigation identifies cause → builder liable for failing to prevent the following-trade damage → roof sheet replacement in affected areas, or early full replacement.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Following trades are briefed before roof work — no grinders over or near finished roofing. Alternative cutting methods are used where penetrations are required. Any inadvertent spark damage is identified before sign-off and documented. Concealment point: Spark damage is small and may not be visible immediately. Corrosion develops over months under the surface of the coating. By the time it is visible, the damage is established. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started

Consequence: Coating damage → corrosion → visible rust patches within 6-18 months → warranty claim → investigation identifies cause → builder liable for failing to prevent the following-trade damage → roof sheet replacement in affected areas, or early full replacement.
source_content.l5: Evidence of completion: Following trades are briefed before roof work — no grinders over or near finished roofing. Alternative cutting methods are used where penetrations are required. Any inadvertent spark damage is identified before sign-off and documented. Concealment point: Spark damage is small and may not be visible immediately. Corrosion develops over months under the surface of the coating. By the time it is visible, the damage is established. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started

Title: Downpipe and Stormwater Drainage Coordination — Trade Interface Decision
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00022: Downpipe and Stormwater Drainage Coordination — Trade Interface Decision. Trigger: Roof downpipe positions are being finalised. Underground stormwater invert locations are being planned or have been installed. The boundary of responsibility between the roofing trade and the stormwater trade must be agreed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Roof drainage design is established. Stormwater connection points are either designed or installed. The builder has confirmed the contract scope of each trade. Selection rule: Coordinate downpipe positions and stormwater invert locations before either system is installed. The builder owns this coordination — it is not the responsibility of either plumbing trade to discover the other's work on site. Failure to coordinate results in misalignment, visible bends, and additional fittings that look unprofessional and reduce hydraulic performance
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Site geometry and available fall; reactive soil risk (increases consequence of poor stormwater); contract scope and trade procurement sequence; whether the builder coordinates trades directly or each trade procures separately. Alternatives: Roofer selects downpipe positions and stormwater trade connects to them wherever they land; stormwater invert positions are fixed first and roofer positions downpipes to suit; positions are coordinated before either trade begins installation; positions are not coordinated and visible offsets/
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No coordination occurs. Roofing completes with downpipes in positions that do not align with stormwater infrastructure. Unsightly bends or serious misalignment at the connection. Consequence: Misaligned connection → additional bends reduce hydraulic performance → partial blockage risk → water diverted in extreme rainfall → pooling near the foundation → reactive soil movement → structural damage to the slab. Alternatively: stormwater not connected at all → water discharging to the surface → neighbour and erosion complaints → council enforcem
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Downpipe positions are agreed before either system is installed. The stormwater plan shows invert locations that align with the roof drainage design. No visible offsets or bends are required at the downpipe-to-stormwater junction. Concealment point: Once the roof is sheeted and the slab/paths are poured, the junction between downpipe and stormwater is physically fixed. Correction requires opening up the ground connection. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not S

Title: Rainwater Tank Operation — Commissioning vs Compliance on Paper
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00023: Rainwater Tank Operation — Commissioning vs Compliance on Paper. Trigger: A dwelling has been built with a requirement for a rainwater retention tank (council-mandated minimum typically 1,000L). The completion/handover stage is reached.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: The tank, pump, connections, and any automatic switchover are specified or installed. Council completion sign-off requirements are defined. The owner has been informed of the system. Selection rule: Council minimum capacity is the floor, not the optimum. Provide connections that are actually commissioned and operational at handover — not capped points waiting for the owner to install the tank later. Automatic switchover reduces the risk of the owner running on empty mains without noticing, but can conceal a non-functioning tank. Design for
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Owner's maintenance capacity and willingness; whether automatic switchover is specified; urban vs rural user (rural users typically maintain rainwater systems actively); tank size relative to average collection from the connected catchment; pump quality and suitability for the expected duty cycle. Alternatives: Install the minimum-compliant tank, pump and connections, leaving operation to the owner; install a higher-capacity tank with automatic switchover and realistic user-interface; provide capped connection points with no tan
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Tank not installed at handover (capped connections only). Or tank installed but pump not commissioned. Owner occupies the dwelling without a functioning rainwater system. Consequence: Non-functioning tank → owner uses mains water for toilet/laundry without awareness → pump burns out (if tank does eventually run) → owner calls for warranty service → investigation reveals system was never properly commissioned → builder liable for incomplete installation. Council sign-off obtained despite incomplete installation is a secondary regulatory fail
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Tank is installed, filled, and pump is operational at practical completion. Switchover (if fitted) is tested. Owner is briefed on basic maintenance. Council completion documentation confirms tank is installed and connected. Concealment point: Once ceiling and cladding are complete, the plumbing connections to the tank are concealed. A non-commissioned system looks identical to a commissioned one from the outside. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/No

Title: Non-Compliant Design — Installer's Obligation to Escalate Before Installation
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00024: Non-Compliant Design — Installer's Obligation to Escalate Before Installation. Trigger: A trade installer receives drawings or a site condition that they believe does not comply with the applicable standard. The non-compliance was not caught by the designer, builder, or certifier upstream.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: The installer has reviewed the plans and/or assessed the site. A specific condition — such as a roof pitch below the minimum for the specified valley arrangement — appears to be non-compliant with the applicable standard. Selection rule: The worst outcome is completing a known non-compliant installation. The installer is not excused by the fact that the designer, builder, or certifier has approved or repeated the detail — each party has their own responsibility at their decision point. Where a non-compliance is identified: stop before inst
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Nature of the non-compliance; certainty of the installer's assessment; consequences of the non-compliance in heavy rainfall; financial and programme pressure to proceed; whether the work is part of a repeat/volume-build where the same error will be replicated. Alternatives: Complete the installation as drawn and let the issue pass; raise the issue with the builder and document the concern; refuse to install the non-compliant detail and provide written notice to the builder.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Installer proceeds with a known non-compliant detail without raising a formal objection. Heavy rainfall events expose the performance failure. Multiple dwellings in a repeat-build subdivision affected. Consequence: Non-compliant roof drainage → heavy rainfall event → flooding of dwellings → investigation identifies the pitch/valley non-compliance → all parties in the design-construction chain examined → installer who completed the work without objecting faces liability even though the non-compliance originated upstream.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Non-compliance is identified before installation. Written notice is provided to the builder. The detail is corrected or an alternative is agreed before installation proceeds. If the builder directs the installer to proceed despite the written concern, that instruction and the installer's objection are both documented. Concealment point: Once installed and subsequent work proceeds (sarking, ceilings, cladding), the non-compliant detail is concealed. The failure is only discovered when a heavy rainfall event exposes the performance

Title: Internal Linings Pre-Start Conditions — Weatherproofing and Trade Readiness
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00025: Internal Linings Pre-Start Conditions — Weatherproofing and Trade Readiness. Trigger: Builder contacts lining fixer to commence internal plasterboard fixing on a residential dwelling.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Lining fixer has received plans and costing information. A site visit or call is made before mobilising. Selection rule: Three preconditions must be confirmed before commencing. First: the roof must be on — no exceptions regardless of builder assurance about timing. Second: external cladding or at minimum sarking wrap must be in place. In summer, wrap-only may be acceptable if no moisture is present; in winter or wet conditions, wrap-only is insufficient and full cladding is preferred. Third: no conflicting trades must be active that would
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Season (winter vs summer — changes acceptable weatherproofing standard); moisture inside the frame; builder time pressure (a common source of pressure to commence early); stage of other trades. Alternatives: Commence work immediately; commence with wrap-only weatherproofing in summer; refuse to commence until conditions are met.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Commencement despite moisture or inadequate weatherproofing — plasterboard absorbs moisture, swells, loses structural integrity, and delaminates from fixings. Consequence: Moisture-affected sheets installed → swelling causes surface irregularity → delamination and nail pops within weeks → full strip-out and re-sheet required → dispute with builder about who bears the cost → lining fixer's reputation and contractor relationship damaged.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Visual inspection on site confirms roof is complete and weathertight. Sarking or cladding is in place on all external walls. No moisture visible on slab or frame. Sheet storage area (garage) is dry. Concealment point: Once lining is installed and moisture is trapped behind it, the damage is not visible until mould appears or the sheets delaminate — which may be months later. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Ceiling Sheeting Sequence — Ceilings Before Walls, Direction From Frame
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00026: Ceiling Sheeting Sequence — Ceilings Before Walls, Direction From Frame. Trigger: Lining fixer is ready to commence sheeting after pre-start checks are complete.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Insulation is in external walls. Flashings are installed at wet area corners. Stud and nog check is complete. Sheets are positioned in the garage. Selection rule: All ceilings are sheeted first across the entire house before any wall sheeting begins. This is a firm rule. Sheet direction must follow the frame direction — sheets run at right angles to the truss bottom chords or ceiling battens. Where roof framing changes direction (such as at hip junctions), the sheet direction must be assessed and followed consistently — changing direction
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Roof framing direction (may change at hips and dormers); ceiling area (large areas over 3 joins wide require backblocking at recess joints); sheet thickness (10mm standard, 13mm for longer spans or commercial). Alternatives: Sheet ceilings first across the whole house before beginning any wall sheeting; sheet walls first then ceilings.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Wall sheeting commenced before ceilings are complete, or ceiling sheet direction changed mid-area. Consequence: Premature wall sheeting → interference with ceiling sheet installation → sheets not properly supported at wall-ceiling junction → cornices cannot conceal the gap cleanly. Direction change in ceiling → visual joint line visible across ceiling at direction change → sanding cannot correct this → strip and re-sheet affected area.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Ceilings are complete and firm before wall sheeting begins. Sheet direction is consistent and follows the frame direction. Large areas have been backblocked before proceeding to walls. Concealment point: Once cornices are installed and surfaces are painted, ceiling direction inconsistencies or missed backblocking may manifest as cracking at joints — difficult to rectify without stripping sections. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Wet Area Substrate Selection — Fibre Cement vs Aquacheck vs Standard Plasterboard
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00027: Wet Area Substrate Selection — Fibre Cement vs Aquacheck vs Standard Plasterboard. Trigger: Lining fixer is sheeting wet area walls — bathroom, ensuite, laundry, or WC.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Building type (residential vs commercial) is confirmed. Waterproofing specification is known. Tiler's tile weight and fixing method are ideally known but often not confirmed at this stage. Selection rule: For residential: fibre cement is the standard selection. It holds its structural integrity better when wet. For commercial: aquacheck or equivalent proprietary board is standard — easier to cut, handle and work with, but entirely dependent on the quality of the waterproofing membrane over it. If the waterproofing fails, aquacheck degrades
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Building type (residential vs commercial — changes the default selection); waterproofing system quality; tile weight (affects fixing centres — see CDO-00028); whether the substrate will ever be accessible again after tiles are installed. Alternatives: Standard plasterboard (not suitable — excluded from wet areas); fibre cement sheet (residential standard — greater integrity when wet); aquacheck or equivalent proprietary wet area board (commercial standard — easier to work with but requires a sound waterproofing system).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Standard plasterboard used in a wet area; or aquacheck used in residential without adequate waterproofing quality assurance. Consequence: Incorrect substrate in wet area → waterproofing membrane applied over inadequate base → membrane cracks at flexing joints → water penetrates → substrate saturates → swells and delaminates → tiles de-bond → full tile strip, substrate replacement, re-waterproof, re-tile. Cost: $5,000–$20,000+ depending on area.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Wet area sheets are confirmed as fibre cement (residential) or approved proprietary board (commercial) before installation. Waterproofing contractor has confirmed their system is compatible with the substrate. Concealment point: Once waterproofing membrane and tiles are installed, the substrate is permanently concealed. Any moisture damage to an incorrect substrate will manifest years later as tile movement, grout cracking, and mould. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not S

Title: Wet Area Fixing Schedule — Screw Spacing by Tile Weight
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00028: Wet Area Fixing Schedule — Screw Spacing by Tile Weight. Trigger: Wet area substrate sheets are being fixed to studs. The tile specification is known or can be determined.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Tile weight (kg/m²) is confirmed from the tile specification. Stud spacing is established. Sheet thickness is confirmed. Selection rule: The fixing schedule must match the tile weight. In residential practice it is common to use the same fixing centres regardless of tile weight — this is non-compliant. The consequences are a substrate that moves under heavy tile loading, grout cracking, and eventual tile de-bonding. The lining fixer must confirm the tile specification before completing the wet area fixing, because once the waterproofing me
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Tile weight per m² (the governing variable); tile format (large format tiles exert different point loads); whether tiles are a future client choice (common in residential — substrate must be fixed to the heavier category to be safe). Alternatives: Up to 12.5 kg/m²: 200mm centres at field, 150mm at butt joints, corners, and openings; 12.5–32 kg/m²: 100mm centres throughout; over 32 kg/m²: engineer's specification required.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Standard 200mm fixing centres used in wet area without checking tile weight. Heavy tiles installed over under-fixed substrate. Consequence: Under-fixed substrate flexes under tile load → grout cracks → water ingress → substrate damage → tiles de-bond → full strip-out. Practitioner acknowledged this was common residential practice — a systemic standards gap.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Fixing schedule is confirmed against the tile specification before installation is completed. Where tile weight is unknown, the 100mm schedule (12.5–32kg/m²) is applied as the conservative default. Concealment point: Once waterproofing membrane and tiles are installed, fixing spacing is permanently inaccessible. Deficient fixing only becomes apparent when tiles begin to de-bond. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Expansion Joint Placement — Ceilings Exceeding 12 Metres
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00029: Expansion Joint Placement — Ceilings Exceeding 12 Metres. Trigger: Lining fixer is planning the ceiling sheet layout for an open-plan area. Total ceiling run in one direction is being assessed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Ceiling plan dimensions are measured. Frame type (timber vs steel) is identified. Total ceiling run in one direction is calculated. Selection rule: Any ceiling run exceeding 12 metres in a single direction requires an expansion joint to accommodate movement of the building structure relative to the lining. The threshold is 12 metres. Joints are typically placed between external wall zones where differential movement is likely. Steel-framed buildings require more careful attention to this requirement than timber-framed buildings because ste
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Total ceiling run (the threshold is 12m); frame type (steel vs timber — changes urgency); whether the building is in a climate with significant temperature range; whether the open plan area crosses a structural zone boundary. Alternatives: No expansion joint (acceptable under 12m); expansion joint at the 12m threshold; additional expansion joints at shorter intervals in steel-framed buildings.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No expansion joint installed in a ceiling run exceeding 12m; or joint placed at wrong location. Consequence: Building movement → ceiling lining cracks at the point of highest stress (typically at the external wall junction or mid-span of the long run) → crack visible through paint → investigation reveals no expansion joint → strip affected section, install joint, re-sheet, re-flush, re-paint.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Ceiling plan is reviewed before sheeting begins. All runs exceeding 12m are identified and expansion joint locations are marked. Joint is installed as sheeting proceeds — it cannot be retrofitted. Concealment point: Once the ceiling is flushed and painted, the absence of an expansion joint is invisible until the ceiling cracks at the location where a joint should have been. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Taping Sequence — All-at-Once vs Second Coat Before Internals
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00030: Taping Sequence — All-at-Once vs Second Coat Before Internals. Trigger: All sheeting is complete. The flusher is planning the taping and flushing sequence.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: All sheets are fixed. Backblocking is complete where required. The flusher's preferred method is established or the site supervisor has specified a method. Selection rule: Both methods are acceptable. The second method — taping recesses and butts first, second coating them flat, then running internals — produces a superior finish on internal corners because the corner is run onto an already-flat surface rather than into the slight deviation left by a taped-and-first-coated recess joint. The first method (tape everything then coat) is faste
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Quality standard required; number of internal corners crossing recess joints; compound type used (setting compound vs all-purpose changes working time). Alternatives: Tape everything first (recesses, butts, internals) then second coat all; tape recesses and butts first, second coat flat, then run internals over the flat second coat surface.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Method changed mid-project; internals run before recesses are sufficiently flat. Consequence: Inconsistent finish at internal corners visible under paint in raking light → client complaint → rectification requires sanding, re-coating, and repainting affected corners.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Joints are taped and flushed with consistent method across the project. No change of method mid-project — this creates visible inconsistency in the finished surface. Concealment point: Taping and flushing are concealed by paint. Deficiencies in the junction between internal corners and recess joints only become visible under raking light after painting. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Compound Selection — All-Purpose vs Chemical-Setting Base Coat
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00031: Compound Selection — All-Purpose vs Chemical-Setting Base Coat. Trigger: Flusher is preparing to begin taping and coating. Compound must be selected before mixing.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Type of work (residential vs commercial); ambient temperature and season; time constraints on the project; number of coats required. Selection rule: The industry trend is toward all-purpose compound for all coats because it eliminates setting time management and allows all coats to be used interchangeably. The trade-off is that all-purpose is air-drying — it relies on airflow and temperature, and in winter can take 48+ hours rather than the stated 24 hours, and in extreme cases 3+ days. Chemical-setting base coat (50, 60, or 90 minute) giv
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Season (winter significantly extends all-purpose drying time); site ventilation; project schedule (fast-track projects favour setting compound); number of coats; cost of compound. Alternatives: Chemical-setting base coat (45, 60, or 90 minute setting time); air-drying all-purpose compound for all coats.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: All-purpose compound used in cold winter conditions — drying time extends to 48–72 hours, delaying sanding and subsequent trades. Consequence: All-purpose applied in winter → 48–72 hour dry time instead of 24 → sanding delayed → painter delayed → whole-of-project programme impact → liquidated damages risk on larger projects.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Compound type is confirmed before mixing begins. All-purpose is not selected for use in winter or on cold, poorly-ventilated sites without confirming acceptable drying times. Sufficient compound is mixed for the working time available. Concealment point: Once applied and dried, incorrect compound selection cannot be changed — but the consequence is typically schedule delay rather than a quality defect. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Verified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.
