Title: Trade Exclusion During Linings — Silica Dust and Sequencing
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00032: Trade Exclusion During Linings — Silica Dust and Sequencing. Trigger: Internal linings fixing, flushing, or sanding is underway. Another trade (cabinetmaker, painter, tiler) attempts to commence work in the same space.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Linings work is active. Another trade is scheduled or is arriving without scheduling. Silica dust may be generated by current activities. Selection rule: No other trade should be working in areas where linings fixing, flushing, or sanding is occurring. The reasons are twofold: practical sequencing (cabinets cannot be installed until sheets are fixed; painters cannot start until flushing is complete and compound is dry) and health — silica dust generated by cutting, sanding, or handling plasterboard products is a regulated hazard with a ver
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Stage of linings work (sanding generates most silica dust); type of intrusive trade; ventilation of the space; project schedule pressure. Alternatives: Allow other trades to work concurrently; exclude other trades until linings are fully complete; allow specific trades to commence in completed areas only.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Another trade works in the same space during sanding — silica dust exposure occurs without respiratory protection. Consequence: Silica exposure → cumulative lung damage → silicosis (irreversible) → WorkCover claim → investigation reveals inadequate site management of silica hazard → builder and lining fixer liable for failure to control the exposure.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: No other trade is present in areas where cutting, sanding, or flushing is active. If a trade arrives unscheduled, they are directed to wait by the site supervisor. Silica controls are in place (respiratory protection, dust suppression or extraction) wherever cutting or sanding occurs. Concealment point: Silica dust is invisible and has no immediate warning symptoms. Cumulative exposure causes silicosis — irreversible and progressive. The concealment is physiological, not physical. Standard reference: not specified; clause verifica

Title: Design Information Sufficiency Before Electrical Layout
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00033: Design Information Sufficiency Before Electrical Layout. Trigger: Builder or client brief received — electrician decides whether enough information exists to quote and design.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Brief received. Plans and/or room use information available to some degree. Selection rule: The electrician must do a reality check rather than accepting the plan literally. Missing outlets, inconvenient switching, and future-use issues must be identified before the layout is locked. Where plans are incomplete, the electrician should flag missing room use, intended appliances, and future provisions as conditional items in the quote. Time spent resolving the brief before quoting is billable and defensible.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Completeness of plans; room use clarity; future-use requirements (solar, battery, EV, C-Bus); builder relationship. Alternatives: Proceed on minimal information; proceed with partial plan and assumptions; refuse to quote until full plan received; develop layout collaboratively with client.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Incomplete brief → assumptions in quote/rough-in → design change → variation/rework or compromised usability. Consequence: Unresolved room use → wrong outlet count installed → lining conceals rough-in → client identifies shortfall → rerouting requires opening lined walls → cost and dispute.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Electrical layout agreed before rough-in. Room use and appliances confirmed. Future provisions included or excluded from scope. Concealment point: Once rough-in is complete and walls are lined, re-routing circuits requires invasive work. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 general design provisions]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Wet Area Electrical Location Verification After Fixture Changes
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00034: Wet Area Electrical Location Verification After Fixture Changes. Trigger: Wet-area fixture moved — electrician must re-check whether electrical point location remains acceptable.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Wet area design substantially resolved. Rough-in completed or planned. Fixture locations known or recently changed. Selection rule: A minor plumbing or design change can invalidate an electrical location. The 500mm zone from a sink or bath is a compliance threshold — 505mm complies, 495mm does not. Any fixture movement must trigger re-check of every electrical location in that wet area against AS/NZS 3000 exclusion zone requirements.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Post-rough-in fixture change; proximity to exclusion zone; zone classification (Zone 0, 1, 2); equipment type available. Alternatives: Accept original location; relocate to compliant position; substitute weatherproof fitting where rules permit.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Fixture moved after rough-in → electrical point non-compliant → late relocation → finish disruption and variation. Consequence: Fixture moves → electrical point in exclusion zone → certifier identifies non-compliance → tiles opened → cable relocated → retile → cost exceeds cost of early re-check.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All electrical locations re-checked against actual post-change fixture positions before second fix. Concealment point: Once wet-area tiles are installed, fixture positions and electrical locations are permanently committed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 wet-area Zones 0, 1, 2]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Temporary and Permanent Site Power Location
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00035: Temporary and Permanent Site Power Location. Trigger: Temporary or permanent site supply being scoped — physical meter/supply route must be chosen.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Site established. Builder controls site. SAPN involvement initiated. Selection rule: Best outcome: position permanent meter board in final location and use as temporary supply, avoiding duplication. Where overhead supply passes trees, driveways, or crane/truck access zones, underground should be considered. Supply location is a construction-logistics decision as much as electrical — the electrician must think about vehicle movement and crane arcs.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Proximity to truck/crane/delivery access; trees near aerial route; SAPN approval constraints; timing of first power need. Alternatives: Temporary meter at dedicated pole; permanent meter in final position used as temporary supply; generator-only early stage.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor location → access conflict or forced relocation → duplicated work/cost; poor route → later protection problem. Consequence: Meter board in crane access zone → crane cannot reach required position → board must be relocated → SAPN disconnection/reconnection → 2-4 week delay.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: SAPN has approved meter board location and supply route. Temporary power active without conflicting with site access. Concealment point: Once meter board is installed and SAPN has made service connection, relocation requires SAPN involvement and additional trenching. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 temporary supply; SAPN service rules outside L6]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Pre-Slab Electrical Provisions
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00036: Pre-Slab Electrical Provisions. Trigger: Footings and reinforcement ready — electrical destinations that must pass through slab about to be concealed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Footing and reinforcement works complete. Slab pour imminent. Selection rule: The slab pour is the most absolute concealment event. Once concrete is placed, any destination requiring a conduit through the slab cannot be served without chasing, demolition, or visible surface routing. A 32mm orange PVC swept-bend conduit costs almost nothing to install before the pour and creates optionality for the building life. It must be secured to reinforcement, raised clear of slab to be visible, and photographed before pour.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Presence of island benches, floor GPOs, pool or spa; uncertainty about future load; timing of pour relative to electrician mobilisation. Alternatives: Install conduit for all identified destinations; install conduit plus oversized provision for futures; defer to surface-mounted solutions after slab.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Missed pre-slab provision → slab conceals route → later need arises → surface conduit, chasing, or demolition required. Consequence: Island bench GPO not provided before pour → bench installed without power → client requests GPO → surface conduit only option → aesthetically unacceptable → variation dispute.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All conduits installed and secured before pour. Photograph taken of conduit in position before concrete placed. Concealment point: Slab pour — once concrete is placed, all penetrations are permanently closed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 conduit/underground provisions]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Domestic Circuit Division and Load Balancing
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00037: Domestic Circuit Division and Load Balancing. Trigger: First-fix circuit plan being established — loads must be distributed across final subcircuits.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Plans confirmed. Appliance types and locations known or reasonably anticipated. Selection rule: AS/NZS 3000 minimum does not prevent a single power circuit serving an entire kitchen. But coffee machine + toaster + kettle + dishwasher on one circuit will nuisance-trip at breakfast daily. Kitchen should have minimum two, preferably three, dedicated power circuits. Bedrooms can be grouped. The difference between minimum-compliant and quality design is invisible to the inspector but profound to the occupant.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Kitchen appliance count; household profile; builder pricing expectations; AS/NZS 3000 minimum. Alternatives: Minimum-compliant single circuit per area; balanced multi-circuit with dedicated high-load circuits; premium zone-specific circuits.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Bare-minimum circuit design → simultaneous loads → repeated tripping → occupant frustration and callbacks. Consequence: Single kitchen circuit → coffee machine + toaster + kettle simultaneously → circuit trips → daily callbacks → circuit redesign requires opening lined walls.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Circuit distribution confirmed before rough-in. High-load appliances have dedicated circuits. Kitchen has minimum two power circuits. Concealment point: Once linings are installed, redistributing circuits requires opening walls. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 minimum subcircuit and kitchen circuit requirements]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

source_content.l3: Conditions and variables: Kitchen appliance count; household profile; builder pricing expectations; AS/NZS 3000 minimum. Alternatives: Minimum-compliant single circuit per area; balanced multi-circuit with dedicated high-load circuits; premium zone-specific circuits.
source_content.l4: Failure mode: Bare-minimum circuit design → simultaneous loads → repeated tripping → occupant frustration and callbacks. Consequence: Single kitchen circuit → coffee machine + toaster + kettle simultaneously → circuit trips → daily callbacks → circuit redesign requires opening lined walls.
source_content.l5: Evidence of completion: Circuit distribution confirmed before rough-in. High-load appliances have dedicated circuits. Kitchen has minimum two power circuits. Concealment point: Once linings are installed, redistributing circuits requires opening walls. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 minimum subcircuit and kitchen circuit requirements]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Cable Routes and Framing Penetrations — Size, Location, Service Separation
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00038: Cable Routes and Framing Penetrations — Size, Location, Service Separation. Trigger: First-fix cables need to pass through framing shared with plumbing, data, and other services.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Frame erected. Plumbing first-fix commenced or planned. Cavity open before lining. Selection rule: The wall cavity is shared territory. Drill at least 25mm from the stud edge, at stud centre where possible, with a hole large enough for future cables. Where plumbing and electrical converge (common in bathrooms), a direct call to the plumber is faster than going through the builder. Always use the opposite face of the stud from the plumber where possible.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Plumbing route; number of cables; stud size; builder approval for larger holes. Alternatives: Minimum-size hole exactly where needed; preferred centre location with future-cable clearance; coordinate with plumber; reroute electrical.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Services crowded into same zone → lining closes → later screw penetrates pipe or cable → water leak or electrical fault. Consequence: Plumbing and electrical converge in bathroom → cabinetmaker fixes vanity → drill through electrical cable → live fault in wet area → emergency rectification → lining, tiles, vanity opened.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Holes positioned at stud centre or at least 25mm from edge. Service separation confirmed with plumber before lining. Routes photographed. Concealment point: Once lining is installed, framing penetrations are permanently concealed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 cable separation; AS 1684 stud penetration limits]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Electric Cooktop Isolation Device Location
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00039: Electric Cooktop Isolation Device Location. Trigger: Kitchen layout known — isolating switch for electric cooktop must be located within actual joinery geometry.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Kitchen layout confirmed. Cooktop type (electric vs gas) confirmed. Joinery design substantially resolved. Selection rule: AS/NZS 3000 requires an isolating device for an electric cooktop that is readily accessible and within arm's reach — for emergency isolation. The kitchen geometry creates the challenge: not in a cupboard, not concealed by fridge or pantry, reachable in an emergency. The electrician must check the actual joinery drawing.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Cooktop type; proximity of fridge, pantry, and joinery; window or splashback position. Alternatives: Readily accessible visible position within arm's reach; joinery location technically compliant but obscured; no separate isolating switch (non-compliant).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poorly located isolation → difficult emergency access or non-compliant installation → rework. Consequence: Isolating switch behind fridge → certifier identifies non-compliance → joinery removed → cable relocated → joinery refitted → delay and variation.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Isolating switch location confirmed against actual joinery drawing before rough-in. Within arm's reach, readily visible, not concealed. Concealment point: Once joinery and finishes are installed, relocating the isolating switch requires reopening the cavity. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 cooktop isolating switch location and accessibility]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Future Electrical Provisions Before Envelope Closure
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00040: Future Electrical Provisions Before Envelope Closure. Trigger: Future loads (solar, battery, EV, patio heaters, spa) plausible but envelope about to close.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: First-fix underway or imminent. Client has not confirmed future requirements but envelope will close. Selection rule: A small investment in spare conduits during first-fix avoids expensive or impossible retrofit later. The building envelope is the key constraint — once a cavity wall is lined on both sides or a rendered wall is complete, routing a new cable requires surface trunking or invasive work. Install 20mm orange conduit for each likely future scenario during first-fix. Cost is negligible. Retrofit cost without provision can be hundr
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Envelope type and sealing sequence; likely future loads; client willingness to pay for provision. Alternatives: Install spare conduits/routes for anticipated future loads; wait for confirmed instruction; compromise by preserving route in meter board area only.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No provision → envelope completed → future system requested → external conduit or invasive retrofit. Consequence: Client requests EV charger 2 years after occupation → cavity wall fully lined → surface trunking only option → aesthetically unacceptable → invasive install → significant cost for a provision that cost $50 during first-fix.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Spare conduits installed for likely future loads before envelope closure. Routes documented and photographed. Concealment point: Once envelope is closed, future provision routes are concealed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No specific AS mapping — accepted practice and expert foresight. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Pre-Lining Evidence Capture — Photographing Electrical Rough-In
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00041: Pre-Lining Evidence Capture — Photographing Electrical Rough-In. Trigger: First-fix rough-in complete — walls about to be lined, permanently concealing all cable routes.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Rough-in complete and inspected. Lining imminent. Selection rule: Photographs of the rough-in are the electrician's record of where every cable, conduit, and penetration is located. They serve three purposes: protect the electrician if a future trade penetrates a cable; guide the second-fix technician to exact outlet locations; demonstrate to the certifier that the installation was completed correctly before concealment.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Upcoming lining programme; complexity of rough-in; number of slab conduits; builder relationship. Alternatives: Photograph every room before lining; rely on drawings and memory; photograph only non-standard installations.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: No photographic record → later trade penetrates cable → dispute → no evidence → cost borne by electrician. Consequence: Cabinetmaker fixes vanity → drill strikes live cable → builder claims cable was not where electrician said → no photos → dispute → WorkCover investigation.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All rooms photographed before lining. Photos retained in project file. Builder notified lining can proceed. Concealment point: Lining installation — once lining is fixed, all cable routes are permanently concealed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No specific AS mapping — accepted practice and risk management. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Electrical Point Survival Through Lining and Tiling Handoff
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00042: Electrical Point Survival Through Lining and Tiling Handoff. Trigger: Lining or tiling about to cover electrical points — they must survive the handoff undamaged.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Rough-in complete. Lining crew or tiler about to commence work near electrical points. Selection rule: The lining and tiling handoff is a common source of electrical damage. A box set slightly too deep when a tile goes over it becomes inaccessible. The electrician should coordinate with the lining fixer and tiler, ensure boxes are at correct setout for finished surface (accounting for tile thickness), and inspect after tiling.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Tile thickness and type; box setout from rough wall; tiler's awareness of electrical box locations. Alternatives: Accept as-is; install box extension rings before lining; coordinate directly with lining fixer and tiler.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Box buried by tiling → second-fix cannot access → tiles removed → retile → delay and variation. Consequence: Tiler tiles over electrical box in wet area → box 15mm below tile surface → second-fix cannot install fitting → tiles must be removed → retile.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All boxes at correct setout for finished surface before tiling. Tiler briefed on box locations. Boxes inspected after tiling before second fix. Concealment point: Once tiles are grouted, electrical box positions are fixed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 box setout and accessibility requirements]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Energisation Readiness — Final Checks Before Connecting to Supply
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00043: Energisation Readiness — Final Checks Before Connecting to Supply. Trigger: Second-fix complete — installation about to be energised and connected to supply for the first time.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Second-fix complete. All fittings, GPOs, switches, and appliances installed. Certifier inspection imminent or complete. Selection rule: The electrical installation must be tested and certified before energisation — a legal requirement under AS/NZS 3000 and SA electrical licensing. Testing includes insulation resistance of every circuit, earthing continuity, RCD tripping time and current, and polarity. Every result must be documented. The Certificate of Electrical Compliance must be provided to the customer before use.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Completeness of second-fix; RCD test results; insulation resistance outcomes; certifier inspection date. Alternatives: Energise and connect; energise after preliminary testing only; energise after full documented testing and certification.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Premature energisation → concealed wiring fault → electrical fault under load → fire or shock → investigation → no certificate → criminal liability. Consequence: Energisation without testing → insulation failure → fire → investigation reveals no test certificate → criminal charges and personal liability.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All tests completed and results recorded. Certificate of Electrical Compliance prepared. Builder notified energisation can proceed. Concealment point: The installation is live. Faults present at testing but missed may cause injury or fire. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 testing and certification; SA Electrical Products Act]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Failed Electrical Test — Fault Finding Before Certification
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00044: Failed Electrical Test — Fault Finding Before Certification. Trigger: A test result has returned outside acceptable limits — cause must be identified before certification.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Testing in progress. A test has failed. Cause is unknown. Selection rule: A failed test result is diagnostic information, not a reason to certify and hope. Isolate the failed circuit, disconnect loads progressively to locate the fault section, identify the specific cause. Common causes: cable nicked during first-fix; moisture in a wet area box; incorrect termination; damaged insulation at framing penetration. Certifying with a known fault is professional and legal negligence.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Fault type; circuit location; accessibility of suspect section; whether lining has been applied. Alternatives: Accept the failed result and certify; isolate failed circuit and certify rest; locate and rectify before certifying any part.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Unresolved fault certified → energisation → fault manifests → fire or shock → investigation → criminal and civil liability. Consequence: Failed insulation resistance test → electrician proceeds → cable fault causes fire → investigation reveals test failure was known → criminal charges and full remediation liability.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Fault located and rectified. All tests re-run and pass. Certificate issued. Fault cause documented. Concealment point: None — a failed test resolved before certification has no downstream consequence. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 testing and remediation; SA Electrical Products Act]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: HVAC Capacity Sizing for Residential Dwelling
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00045: HVAC Capacity Sizing for Residential Dwelling. Trigger: Plans and brief received — HVAC system capacity must be sized for the dwelling.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Plans available. Building type, orientation, and client budget known. Selection rule: Air conditioning sizing is an exact science plus or minus 20%. In volume homes, budget constraints typically drive selection to approximately 80% of calculated peak load. This means the system meets most demand but cannot achieve target temperature on extreme days (45 degrees C+). This accepted commercial trade-off should be disclosed to the client. Orientation affects load by approximately 10%.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Building orientation; volume home vs custom; whether client has been advised about capacity shortfall on extreme days. Alternatives: Full J-calculation to peak load; manufacturer/supplier software to 100% load; pragmatic sizing to approximately 80% of calculated load.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Undersizing for cost → acceptable operation most of year → extreme-day shortfall → temperature cannot reach target → dissatisfaction. Consequence: 80% capacity system → 45 degree day → system runs continuously → indoor stabilises at 27 degrees rather than 22 → occupant complaint → unit replacement required.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: System capacity calculated using accepted method. Client informed if capacity is below peak theoretical load. Concealment point: Once equipment is ordered and installed, upsizing requires replacing indoor and outdoor units and potentially modifying ductwork. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 Vol 2 H6 HVAC energy efficiency provisions]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: HVAC First Fix Readiness — Building State Before Ductwork
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00046: HVAC First Fix Readiness — Building State Before Ductwork. Trigger: Builder ready for HVAC rough-in — technician must decide whether building conditions are sufficient to start.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Builder has notified HVAC technician that first-fix is scheduled. Selection rule: Copper refrigerant pipe has significant theft value. HVAC materials should not be on site until the building is secure. Ideal starting condition is lock-up: roof on, external walls clad, doors and windows in. Internal walls must be unlined to allow duct and pipe routes. HVAC technician typically works at the same time as electrician and plumber on first-fix.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Site security; weather exposure of equipment; whether internal walls are already lined. Alternatives: Commence at full lock-up; commence at partial lock-up; defer to full lock-up.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Too early → copper pipe theft; too late → concealed routes unavailable → surface trunking required. Consequence: HVAC first-fix before lock-up → copper pipe stolen → replacement cost plus programme delay.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Building at lock-up or confirmed secure. Internal walls unlined. First-fix proceeds. Concealment point: Once internal linings and ceilings are installed, concealed routes are closed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No specific AS mapping — accepted practice and site security judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Roof Structural Support for Indoor HVAC Unit
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00047: Roof Structural Support for Indoor HVAC Unit. Trigger: Indoor HVAC unit to be supported in or under roof structure — permanent load must be accommodated.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: HVAC system selected and indoor unit weight known. Truss design complete or under review. Selection rule: Modern residential roof trusses are not designed for permanent dead load of an HVAC indoor unit. A person standing briefly on a truss is a live load; a 50-100kg HVAC unit sitting permanently is a dead load the truss was not designed to carry. The builder must ensure the structural engineer or truss manufacturer has designed a specific support location for the unit at the correct position.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Unit mass and position (must match structural design); whether builder has coordinated with structural engineer; whether truss shop drawings specify an HVAC support. L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Truss design or structural design specifically provides for HVAC unit dead load at nominated position. Concealment point: Once unit is installed and ceilings are in, structural deflection is difficult to observe and hard to rectify. Title: Return Air and Supply Outlet Location
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00048: Return Air and Supply Outlet Location. Trigger: Supply and return-air locations being laid out relative to rooms, doors, occupancy, and performance requirements.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: System capacity confirmed. Duct layout being designed. Selection rule: A return air path that relies on open doors is unreliable — occupants will close bedroom doors. Return air intake should be in circulation space or near high-use areas. Supply outlets should be positioned where they can mix air across the room. Kitchens do not require a dedicated outlet.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Bedroom door usage patterns; open-plan vs compartmentalised; noise-sensitive rooms adjacent to indoor unit. Alternatives: Symmetrical geometric layout; occupancy-driven layout; noise-optimised layout.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor return/supply layout → restricted circulation or uneven airflow → under-performance, noise, or comfort complaints. Consequence: Return air in bedroom corridor → occupant closes doors → return path closes → system loses efficiency → repeated service calls → airflow rebalancing cannot fully resolve.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Return air has viable unrestricted path when all bedroom doors are closed. Supply outlets in occupied zones with adequate airflow mixing. Concealment point: Once ceilings and ductwork are installed, relocating outlets requires opening ceilings. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No specific AS mapping — accepted practice and expert design judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Duct Route Selection — Straightness, Bends, and Excess Length
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00049: Duct Route Selection — Straightness, Bends, and Excess Length. Trigger: Ductwork route being selected — bends, lengths, and restrictions may affect delivered airflow.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Outlet positions confirmed. Roof space accessible for duct installation. Selection rule: Every bend in flexible duct adds airflow resistance. A 90-degree bend in 250mm duct is equivalent to approximately 2-3 metres of straight duct. Excess duct not cut but left coiled acts as a restriction. The diagnostic for a poorly performing outlet is almost always a bent or bunched duct — straightening and cutting to length often resolves the problem. Duct must be supported to maintain circular cross-section.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Roof geometry (hips force bends); distance to outlet; excess duct from coil; truss layout. Alternatives: Straight direct route (best); minimal bends; follows roof geometry with multiple bends; leave excess duct coiled in roof (worst).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor routing/support → reduced effective diameter/resistance → low airflow or whistling → comfort complaint → roof-space rework. Consequence: Bedroom duct with 3 bends → airflow 30% of design → uncomfortable → service call → technician straightens duct → airflow restores.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Duct route as straight as practicable. Excess duct cut rather than coiled. Duct supported at regular intervals. Concealment point: Once ceilings are installed, accessing ductwork requires opening ceiling panels. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS 4254 ductwork for air conditioning systems]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Refrigerant Pipework Route and Joint Location
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00050: Refrigerant Pipework Route and Joint Location. Trigger: Refrigerant pipe route and joint locations being selected before wall or ceiling enclosure conceals them.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: HVAC first-fix underway. Wall cavities and ceiling space open. Selection rule: Joints in refrigerant pipework must be accessible for maintenance. A braze joint concealed in an inaccessible roof corner creates permanent maintenance liability. The route should be planned so any necessary joint is at an accessible location. Running through wall cavity in a new build is strongly preferred. Insulation and vapour seal on suction line is critical — vermin eat insulation, and the exposed suction line runs near dew point.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Wall cladding state; pipe coil length vs run distance; accessible joint locations; vermin risk in roof space. Alternatives: Concealed route through wall cavity (preferred); external trunking (where wall already clad); joints at accessible positions; joints concealed in inaccessible roof space (avoid).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor route/joint location → inaccessible leak point → difficult repair; insulation failure → condensation/water damage. Consequence: Joint in inaccessible roof corner develops leak → system loses charge → ceiling must be opened → joint repaired → ceiling patched → significant cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Pipe route confirmed before installation. Necessary joints at accessible locations. Insulation and vapour seal complete. Concealment point: Once wall linings and ceilings installed, pipe routes and joints concealed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 1677 refrigerant systems; refrigerant code of practice outside L6]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Pre-Commissioning Integrity Gate — Nitrogen Test and Vacuum
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00051: Pre-Commissioning Integrity Gate — Nitrogen Test and Vacuum. Trigger: Refrigerant pipework complete — circuit must be demonstrated leak-tight and dry before commissioning.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: All refrigerant pipework complete. Flare connections made. System ready for pressure and vacuum testing. Selection rule: Pre-commissioning sequence is non-negotiable: nitrogen pressure test first (dry nitrogen, not compressed air which contains moisture), hold 24 hours, then evacuate to below 500 microns (aim for 100 microns or better). Nitrogen is used because it is dry — compressed air contains moisture that reacts with refrigerant or freezes at the expansion device. The system must not be commissioned until the vacuum target is achieved
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Refrigerant type (changes test pressure); duration of nitrogen hold; whether vacuum holds at target. Alternatives: Pressure test and evacuate before commissioning; skip pressure test and proceed to vacuum only; commission without testing (non-compliant and dangerous).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Leak or moisture left in system → refrigerant admitted → poor performance, blockage, or release → callback and repair. Consequence: System commissioned without vacuum → residual moisture → reacts with refrigerant oil → acid forms in compressor → compressor fails at 2 years → full system replacement.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Nitrogen test passes 24-hour hold. Vacuum achieves and holds below 500 microns. Refrigerant valves opened only after vacuum confirmed. Concealment point: The refrigerant circuit is opened and the system commissioned. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 1677 refrigerant system integrity testing; refrigerant code of practice thresholds not L6]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Refrigerant Selection — Service Life and Phase-Down Implications
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00052: Refrigerant Selection — Service Life and Phase-Down Implications. Trigger: Equipment and refrigerant platform being selected — long-term serviceability and regulatory change implications.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Equipment selection being made. Refrigerant type of selected equipment known. Selection rule: The refrigerant used in a system determines its service characteristics for its entire 10-15 year life. R22 is effectively unavailable at reasonable cost due to phase-down. R410A has GWP of approximately 2000 and is subject to Australian HFC phase-down. R32 is the current industry transition. Hydrocarbon refrigerants have very low GWP but are classified as flammable. A system with R410A may face increasing recharge costs as phase-down progresses.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Phase-down schedule and current cost trajectory; client's intended system life; technical handling requirements. Alternatives: Select R410A (high GWP, being phased out); select R32 (current industry transition); select low-GWP hydrocarbon (low GWP, flammable, emerging).
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: System selected for current cost → phase-down progresses → recharge cost increases → long-term cost higher than expected. Consequence: R410A system installed in 2026 → phase-down accelerates → R410A recharge cost increases 3-5x → 2035 service call → recharge cost exceeds system value → early replacement required.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Equipment selection confirmed. Client advised of refrigerant type and phase-down implications. Concealment point: Once equipment installed, refrigerant platform is fixed for system life. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — Australian HFC phase-down legislation; AS/NZS refrigerant safety classification]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Refrigerant Leak Response — Controlled Handling and PPE
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00053: Refrigerant Leak Response — Controlled Handling and PPE. Trigger: Refrigerant being handled during connection, disconnection, or service — liquid and high-pressure gas contact risk must be managed.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Refrigerant work being performed. Equipment pressurised with refrigerant. Selection rule: Liquid refrigerant contact with skin causes cold burn — a chemical burn that can require weeks of treatment. Standard gloves provide limited protection against high-pressure liquid refrigerant spray. Best protection is controlled work practice: use quick-connect fittings wherever possible, work slowly and deliberately, minimise time that a pressurised fitting is open. Quick-connect fittings have largely replaced open-ended flare connections in modern
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Pressure of refrigerant circuit; availability of quick-connect fittings; volume of refrigerant; experience level of technician. Alternatives: Standard gloves and normal practice; quick-connect fittings to minimise release; slow deliberate connections with standard PPE.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Uncontrolled refrigerant release → liquid contact with skin → cold burn → weeks off work → WorkCover claim. Consequence: Technician removes flare from pressurised circuit without depressurising → liquid refrigerant sprays onto hand → cold burn → hospitalisation → 4 weeks off work → WorkCover investigation → penalty for contractor.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Quick-connect fittings used wherever possible. Technician wearing appropriate PPE. Connections made slowly and deliberately. Concealment point: None — controlled practice prevents exposure. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — WHS Regulations SA Part 7 hazardous chemicals; Safe Work Australia PPE code]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Authorisation and Supervision for Refrigerant and HVAC Work
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00054: Authorisation and Supervision for Refrigerant and HVAC Work. Trigger: Task involving refrigerant handling is being allocated — who is authorised and sufficiently supervised.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Job being allocated. Worker's licence status and competency level known. Selection rule: Refrigerant handling in Australia requires an ARCtick licence. An apprentice may perform HVAC work under supervision, but the licensed technician must be present and able to intervene for any task involving live refrigerant. Vacuum and pressure testing, connection of refrigerant lines, and commissioning are not tasks an apprentice should perform unsupervised.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Apprentice stage and training; task type (refrigerant-live vs non-live); availability of licensed technician; client urgency. Alternatives: Allocate to fully licensed and authorised technician; supervise apprentice under licensed technician; defer task until licensed technician present.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Unlicensed refrigerant handling → WorkSafe investigation → licence suspension → cost and penalty. Consequence: Apprentice connects refrigerant lines unsupervised → error → refrigerant release → client property damage → investigation → company loses ARCtick licence → business cannot perform HVAC work.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All refrigerant-live tasks performed by or under direct supervision of ARCtick-licensed technician. Concealment point: None — correct authorisation prevents liability. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — ARCtick licensing; Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Outdoor Unit Location — Access, Clearance, Noise, and Planning
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00055: Outdoor Unit Location — Access, Clearance, Noise, and Planning. Trigger: Outdoor unit position being selected relative to building footprint, site boundaries, and operational requirements.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Building footprint and site layout known. System capacity confirmed. Outdoor unit dimensions and sound power known. Selection rule: Outdoor unit location involves four constraint sets: manufacturer clearances; acoustic impact on neighbours; local council setback and noise requirements; and maintenance access. A unit acceptable in daytime may not meet council night-time limits near a neighbour's bedroom window. Very long pipe runs from the indoor unit also affect refrigerant charge and may exceed manufacturer line-length limits.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Distance to neighbour habitable room; unit sound power; council acoustic requirements; manufacturer clearances; pipe run length. Alternatives: Position at most convenient location for pipework; optimised for clearance and access; minimises neighbour noise impact; constrained by council requirements.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor location → noise complaint → council enforcement → relocation required. Consequence: Outdoor unit adjacent to neighbour's bedroom → night-time operation breaches council limit → noise complaint → council notice → relocation → pipe connections remade → additional refrigerant charge.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Outdoor unit position satisfies manufacturer clearances, council requirements, and acoustic impact assessment. Concealment point: Once outdoor unit installed and pipework connected, relocation is expensive and requires remaking pipe connections. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — council planning; AS/NZS 2107 acoustic requirements for residential buildings]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Pipe Line Length and Factory Precharge
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00056: Pipe Line Length and Factory Precharge. Trigger: HVAC system layout being planned — pipe run length must be checked against manufacturer's precharge allowance.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Outdoor and indoor unit positions confirmed. Pipe route length can be calculated. Selection rule: Split system units are factory precharged for a standard pipe run length (typically 5-7 metres). For every additional metre, additional refrigerant must be added per manufacturer specification. A system without the required additional refrigerant will underperform and may damage the compressor. The pipe length calculation must account for the actual route including bends and vertical rise.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Actual pipe route length vs precharge standard; whether additional refrigerant has been calculated; manufacturer maximum line length. Alternatives: Accept system within precharge allowance; calculate and add additional refrigerant per manufacturer specification; redesign to reduce run length.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Under-charged system → compressor runs hot → reduced efficiency and life → early failure → warranty dispute. Consequence: Pipe run of 12m vs 5m precharge → no additional refrigerant → undercharged → compressor fails at 3 years → manufacturer cites incorrect charge → costs borne by installer.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Pipe run length calculated before installation. Additional refrigerant requirement determined. System charged to correct total charge. Concealment point: Once system commissioned, incorrect charge affects compressor life and performance. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Manufacturer specification (not AS); [CHECK — AS/NZS 1677 if applicable to charge calculation]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Airflow Balance Verification at Commissioning
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00057: Airflow Balance Verification at Commissioning. Trigger: System commissioned — airflow to each outlet must be verified and balanced.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: System running. All outlets connected. Ductwork and ceilings complete. Selection rule: Airflow balance ensures each outlet receives its design volume of air. Without balancing, rooms close to indoor unit receive excess airflow while remote rooms receive insufficient flow. Balancing requires adjusting motorised or manual dampers on each branch. If a room does not perform acceptably after damper adjustment, the duct route should be inspected for bends, crushing, or excess length.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: System size and complexity; whether motorised dampers installed; whether client complaint received. Alternatives: Commission and leave without measuring; measure total system airflow only; measure and balance individual outlet airflow against design.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor airflow balance → room under-performance → complaint → service call → adjustment → avoidable callback. Consequence: Bedroom at end of duct run receives insufficient airflow → client complains → technician enters roof space → discovers 3 90-degree bends → straightens duct → airflow restores.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All rooms achieve approximately equal temperature at set-point. Any under-performing room investigated. Concealment point: None — balancing issues can be rectified at commissioning without opening any structure. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS 4254 duct balancing; manufacturer commissioning requirements]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Condensate Drain Discharge Location
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00058: Condensate Drain Discharge Location. Trigger: Condensate drain route and discharge point for indoor unit must be selected during first-fix.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Indoor unit position confirmed. Building drainage layout known. Selection rule: A ducted indoor HVAC unit in cooling mode can produce 10-20 litres of condensate per day. This must drain to a point that does not cause water damage or nuisance. Ideal discharge is to plumbing drain. Where gravity is not available, a condensate pump is required. Discharge to outside is acceptable where it does not create ponding, ice, or water damage risk. Condensate drain must be insulated where it passes through warm areas to prevent condensation on the outs
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Indoor unit height relative to drain connections; condensate volume; whether pump is required. Alternatives: Gravity to plumbing drain; gravity to outside; condensate pump where gravity insufficient.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Inadequate condensate drain → overflow → water damage to ceiling and wall → ceiling must be opened. Consequence: Condensate drain connects to blocked external pipe → overflow at indoor unit → water drips onto ceiling lining → ceiling stains and damage → ceiling opened → drain rectified → ceiling replaced.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Condensate drain route confirmed before ceiling closure. Discharge point does not create water damage risk. Drain is insulated where required. Concealment point: Once ceiling is closed, condensate drain is concealed and access is limited. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3500 if condensate discharges to plumbing; manufacturer drain requirements]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: HVAC Work Stoppage — When Conditions Are Unsafe
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00059: HVAC Work Stoppage — When Conditions Are Unsafe. Trigger: HVAC work underway — conditions identified that make continuing unsafe.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Work in progress. Hazard has been identified. Selection rule: The HVAC trade involves a uniquely broad range of hazards: high-voltage electrical work; high-pressure refrigerant; working in hot confined roof spaces; chemical exposure; working at height. The default should be to stop when in doubt. The right escalation path is to the builder for site hazards, to the licensed electrician for electrical isolation questions, and to WorkSafe SA for hazards that cannot be resolved through the normal chain of command.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Type and immediacy of hazard; whether controls can be implemented; supervision available; contractor WHS policy. Alternatives: Continue with additional caution; stop work and address hazard before continuing; stop work and remove from site; notify builder and wait for resolution.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Continuing work with known hazard → incident → injury → investigation → penalty. Consequence: Technician identifies live conductors in roof space → continues work → contacts conductor → electrocution → death → criminal prosecution for failure to provide safe working conditions.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Hazard identified. Work stops. Hazard communicated to responsible party. Work recommences only when hazard is controlled. Concealment point: None — stopping work for safety is always correct. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — WHS Act SA s.17 PCBU duty; WHS Regulations SA Part 4.4 falls; Safe Work Australia roof work code]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Bathroom Fixture and Layout Change Window
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00060: Bathroom Fixture and Layout Change Window. Trigger: Client proposes bathroom fixture or layout change relative to planned first-fix plumbing.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Design substantially resolved. First-fix plumbing planned or underway. Selection rule: A seemingly simple aesthetic change — replacing a back-to-wall toilet with a wall-hung model — has direct structural and plumbing consequences. The wall-hung cistern requires a cavity with specific depth (minimum 150mm rather than 100mm), structural noggins or a dedicated mounting frame, and a tiled access panel. Once the waste penetration is installed and the frame is built, changing the toilet type is not a minor adjustment.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Stage of plumbing first-fix; wall cavity state; client's timeline for decision. Alternatives: Change fixture type and accept plumbing modification; retain original fixture and layout; modify design to work within existing waste position.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Late fixture change → existing waste or cavity no longer suits → redesign or invasive plumbing/framing alteration → cost and delay. Consequence: Client changes from back-to-wall to wall-hung after first-fix → waste position incompatible → framing modified → plumber relocates waste → retile floor → significant cost and delay.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Fixture type confirmed before first-fix waste positions are established. Concealment point: Once slab and first-fix waste penetrations complete, fixture type changes constrained by existing waste position. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 sanitary plumbing; AS/NZS 3500.2 fixture connection]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Tile Size and Layout Selection for Wet Areas
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00061: Tile Size and Layout Selection for Wet Areas. Trigger: Wet-area tile size, orientation, and set-out being chosen against actual falls, drains, and room geometry.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Room geometry confirmed. Drain type and position confirmed. Floor level and falls known. Selection rule: Tile size and floor falls interact directly — a very large format tile (600x1200) is difficult to cut to achieve required fall without large visible obviously non-level pieces. The room dimensions determine how many full tiles can be achieved before a cut. The set-out should be worked back from the most visually prominent fixed element (bath face, entry, shower head wall) rather than from a corner.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Floor fall requirements; room width and length; ceiling height; bath or shower position. Alternatives: Large format tiles (challenging for falls); medium tiles with standard bond; smaller tiles with flexible set-out; mosaic for complex geometry.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Inappropriate tile size/set-out → awkward cuts or inability to achieve falls → poor drainage or appearance → strip-out required. Consequence: Large format tiles selected → floor fall cannot be achieved without significant cutting → tiler advises cannot achieve even fall → strip drain specified → floor screed modified → delay and variation.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Tile size, bond, and set-out confirmed before waterproofing. Set-out drawing shows cut tile sizes at all terminations. Concealment point: Once waterproofing and screed installed, floor fall is fixed. Once tiles installed, set-out is fixed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 Vol 2 wet area; AS 3740 waterproofing; AS/NZS 4671 floor falls]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Bathroom and Task Lighting Position
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00062: Bathroom and Task Lighting Position. Trigger: Bathroom or task lighting positions being developed relative to user, mirror, and activities.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Electrical rough-in being planned. Ceiling/wall positions can still be changed. Selection rule: Light that illuminates the ceiling or the back of the user's head does not illuminate the face for grooming. The light source should be between the user and the mirror — either directly above and slightly forward, or positioned to reflect off the mirror surface toward the face. A downlight at ceiling midpoint above the user's head creates the worst possible shadow. All wet-area downlights must be positioned within AS/NZS 3000 zone rules.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Mirror position; room dimensions; wet-area electrical zone exclusions; whether wall-mounted luminaires acceptable. Alternatives: Geometric ceiling grid; task-focused positioning (between user and mirror or slightly behind and angled); wall-mounted task light flanking mirror.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Geometric lighting layout → user face shadowed → poor experience → additional fittings post-occupation. Consequence: Downlight at midpoint above vanity → shadow falls on face → grooming difficult → client requests additional wall fitting → sparky opens ceiling to run circuit → patch, repaint.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Lighting positions confirmed with electrician before rough-in. Position illuminates task area. Wet-area zone compliance confirmed. Concealment point: Once ceiling rough-in is complete and linings installed, moving a lighting point requires opening the ceiling. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 wet-area zone requirements for luminaire positions]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Palette Coherence — Managing Whites and Undertones Across Finishes
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00063: Palette Coherence — Managing Whites and Undertones Across Finishes. Trigger: Exterior and interior materials being assembled into a coherent palette across different finishes and application types.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Exterior selections established. Internal finishes being selected. Selection rule: The word white covers a perceptual range that includes blue-undertoned, yellow-undertoned, grey-undertoned, and neutral whites. Under artificial and natural light these read differently. The controlling principle is to start from the most constrained selection (exterior palette) and work inward. A single white should be used throughout — on walls, skirtings, cornices, and internal doors — accepting that sheen differences are intentional distinctions within o
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Undertone of each white finish; application type (paint, enamel, two-pack produce different sheens); natural light orientation. Alternatives: Select everything independently from showroom sample boards; develop palette starting from exterior and working inward; compare all selections adjacent before approval.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Uncoordinated selections → adjacent finishes reveal undertone clashes → interior looks inconsistent → repainting or accepted defect. Consequence: Two-pack joinery in warm white and wall paint in cool white installed side by side → clash visible under pendant lights → client requests repaint → entire house repainted at significant cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All white finishes in palette from same base colour (same undertone). All selections viewed adjacent before approval. Ceiling white matches wall white. Concealment point: Once painting and joinery finishes applied, re-selection requires repainting or replacement. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — expert perceptual design judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Client Colour Preference vs Designer Judgement
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00064: Client Colour Preference vs Designer Judgement. Trigger: Client requests a colour or style the designer personally dislikes — brief must still be resolved professionally.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Client brief received. Colour preference conflicting with designer's taste has been expressed. Selection rule: Professional interior design is not the designer imposing their aesthetic. It is answering the client's brief — including briefs that express preferences the designer finds challenging. Colour theory provides the framework for making difficult briefs work: a challenging client colour can almost always be made coherent through choice of supporting colours, undertone matching, material texture, and scale of application.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Whether client preference conflicts with a functional constraint; whether preference has been considered; client's ability to articulate why they want the colour. Alternatives: Substitute designer's preferred colour and present as recommendation; accept client's preference without analysis; analyse preference and develop supporting palette that makes it work.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Designer overrides brief → client receives home that does not reflect preference → client dissatisfied → relationship failure. Consequence: Designer substitutes preferred palette → client notices preference was not followed → trust is lost → client instructs repaint at designer's cost → professional reputation damaged.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Designer presents palette that incorporates client's preference with supporting selections. Client approves complete palette before procurement. Concealment point: None — this is a brief interpretation decision, not a construction decision with a concealment point. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — professional design judgement and ethics. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Kitchen Configuration for Actual Use
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00065: Kitchen Configuration for Actual Use. Trigger: Kitchen plan being resolved around actual daily use, storage, appliances, and service positions.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Floor plan confirmed. Appliance types known or determinable. Selection rule: The kitchen work triangle requires interpretation for modern open-plan kitchens. The butler's pantry addresses the tension between visual cleanliness and operational practicality. The island bench should be sized for its actual function. Storage at point-of-use is more important than total storage volume. The designer imagines repeated everyday movement and maintenance, not only the rendered composition.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Whether client does daily cooking or weekend entertaining; whether they want everything visible or hidden; island bench dimensions relative to kitchen volume. Alternatives: Optimise work triangle only; optimise work triangle with appliance and storage integration; prioritise visual composition; develop custom layout based on client profile.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor ergonomic arrangement → repeated unnecessary movement or functional conflict → dissatisfaction and difficult post-completion alteration. Title: Kitchen Exhaust Ducting and Window Splashback Interface
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00066: Kitchen Exhaust Ducting and Window Splashback Interface. Trigger: Kitchen exhaust route or window-splashback concept proposed — construction and maintenance consequences must be resolved.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Kitchen design substantially resolved. Wall positions confirmed. External wall proximity known. Selection rule: Ducting to atmosphere is always preferred over recirculation. Where an external wall is immediately behind the cooktop, a direct duct penetration is the simplest solution. A window used as a splashback is a contemporary aesthetic choice that requires detailed resolution: the window sill and reveal must be waterproof and cleanable, and the occupant must understand that greasy steam will coat the glass and be visible from outside w
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Whether rangehood is on external wall; duct route length through ceiling space; window position relative to cooktop; client's willingness to maintain. Alternatives: Recirculating rangehood; direct external wall duct (most efficient); roof space exit duct; window as splashback.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Poor extraction → odour and moisture persist; poorly resolved window splashback → cleaning complaints → callbacks. Consequence: Recirculating rangehood above gas cooktop → cooking smells cannot escape → house fills with odours → client demands replacement → wall penetration required in completed kitchen → tiling disturbed.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Extraction route confirmed before first-fix. Window splashback details (sill, reveal, drainage) resolved before installation. Concealment point: Once joinery and wall finishes complete, adding or rerouting extraction requires invasive work. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 kitchen ventilation provisions; AS 1668 mechanical air handling]. Title: Specification vs Display Home — What Must Be Explicitly Included
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00067: Specification vs Display Home — What Must Be Explicitly Included. Trigger: Feature seen in display home assumed to be included — actual construction specification must be established.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Client has visited a display home or provided brief based on rendered images. Selection rule: Display homes are fit-out with maximum upgrades to create the most compelling sales environment. A client who visits a display home and enters a contract for a similar-priced house is typically receiving approximately 60-70% of what they saw. Every item must be documented in a schedule cross-referenced against the contract inclusions. Floor-to-ceiling tiles vs 1200mm height is the most common dispute.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Whether client has visited a display home significantly above their contracted specification; extent of upgrade items; client's budget for upgrades. Alternatives: Accept client's assumption that display home represents inclusions; clarify standard inclusion and identify upgrades; document both in specification.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Visual expectation → unspecified upgrade omitted → completed house differs from assumed display → dispute, disappointment, and variation. Consequence: Client assumes floor-to-ceiling tiles based on display → standard specification is 1200mm → builder installs 1200mm → client disputes → builder provides upgrade at own cost or client pays → commercial damage.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: All inclusions documented in selection schedule. Items differing from display home explicitly noted. Client signs off knowing what is and is not included. Concealment point: Once procurement proceeds against the specification, builder and supplier rely on what is documented. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — professional communication and contract management. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Joinery Measurement Timing — When to Measure for Fabrication
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00068: Joinery Measurement Timing — When to Measure for Fabrication. Trigger: Joinery fabrication about to be ordered — measurement timing relative to construction progress must be determined.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Framing and rough-in complete. Lining installed or about to be installed. Selection rule: Joinery is dimensionally precise — a door opening that is 820mm after framing may be 795mm after lining and casing. Robes, kitchens, and vanities fabricated from framing dimensions without accounting for lining thickness will not fit. The correct approach is to measure from the as-built lining — not drawings, not framing, but the finished plasterboard surface. Where programme pressure pushes for early measurement, the joiner's dimensions must account
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Programme pressure from builder; lining contractor's schedule; floor finish thickness where relevant to vanity height. Alternatives: Measure from framing before lining (faster but risks errors); measure after lining is complete and set (accurate but delays fabrication); measure after lining but before floor finish.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Early measurement → wrong dimensions → joinery does not fit → refabrication or modification → delay and cost. Consequence: Kitchen joinery measured from framing → lining installed → island bench 45mm too wide → cannot be installed → refabrication required → 6-week delay.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Joinery measurement confirmed from as-built lining surfaces. Dimensions cross-checked against design drawing before fabrication commences. Concealment point: Once joinery fabricated, incorrect dimensions require refabrication or on-site modification — both expensive. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — professional sequencing judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: NCC Energy Allowance for Lighting
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00069: NCC Energy Allowance for Lighting. Trigger: Lighting scheme being proposed — must be checked against NCC energy efficiency provisions.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Electrical rough-in being planned. NatHERS assessment underway or complete. Selection rule: NCC 2022 Volume Two Part H6 establishes lighting efficiency requirements for residential buildings as part of the energy efficiency provisions. LED luminaires generally meet the efficiency requirements more easily than halogen alternatives. Feature pendants, decorative fittings, and some specialty luminaires may have lower efficacy. The designer's role is to ensure the selected luminaire schedule satisfies the applicable requirement and any variance
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: NatHERS assessment methodology; whether state adoption of NCC 2022 is current; luminaire efficacy of selected fittings. Alternatives: Design all lighting for maximum visual effect regardless of wattage; design to NCC maximum wattage per square metre; design to target satisfying NCC and delivering desired ambience.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Non-compliant lighting → NatHERS assessment cannot be passed → occupation certificate cannot be issued → luminaire changes required after installation. Consequence: Decorative pendant fittings below NCC H6 threshold → NatHERS assessor cannot certify → electrician must replace fittings → replacement fittings do not match design intent → design compromise.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Luminaire schedule cross-checked against NCC H6 requirements before procurement. Non-compliant fixtures substituted. Concealment point: Once rough-in installed and fittings specified, changing luminaire types may require new positions or fittings. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 Vol 2 H6D4 and H6D5 lighting energy provisions; current SA NatHERS methodology]. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Pre-Order Schedule QA — Door and Product Schedules
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00070: Pre-Order Schedule QA — Door and Product Schedules. Trigger: Long door or product schedule about to be relied upon for ordering — hidden copy/paste or transcription errors must be detected.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Schedule complete and about to be issued for procurement. Selection rule: Copy/paste fatigue is a predictable failure mechanism in long repetitive schedules. A designer who creates a 40-door schedule by duplicating and editing rows will almost certainly miss at least one error. The most common errors are adjacent dimension variants differing by one character (920 vs 820 vs 720), copy errors on handing (left vs right swing), and reference mismatches. The correct quality check is to read the schedule with fresh eyes — ideally a day after pre
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Document length; degree of repetition; time pressure; availability of second reviewer. Alternatives: Issue schedule as completed without independent review; have a colleague review with fresh eyes; read entire document systematically with a printed copy.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Schedule typo → wrong product ordered → opening mismatch → replacement and delay. Consequence: 820 door specified instead of 920 → door fabricated → arrives on site → 100mm narrower than required → does not meet disabled access requirements → reorder → 6-week delay.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Schedule reviewed by a second person or with fresh eyes before procurement. Reviewer confirms each dimension against floor plan independently. Concealment point: Once product ordered and fabricated, incorrect items require reordering and typically a 4-8 week delay. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — professional QA practice. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Dark External Door and Solar Exposure Risk
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00071: Dark External Door and Solar Exposure Risk. Trigger: Dark-coloured external door or finish proposed in high-solar-exposure location.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Door selection being made. Site orientation is known. Selection rule: Dark finishes (particularly black, LRV under 10) on north-facing doors in Adelaide can reach surface temperatures of 80-90 degrees C in direct summer sun, causing paint blistering, timber warping, hardware malfunction, and seal failure. A portico of at least 1500mm depth substantially reduces direct exposure. Manufacturer warranties typically exclude damage from solar exposure beyond their stated limits. The designer who approves a black door on a north-facing facade wit
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Door orientation (north-facing highest risk); shading depth; door material and finish; client determination. Alternatives: Accept dark finish and advise client of risk; accept dark finish with portico of at least 1500mm depth; advise against dark finish and recommend alternative; accept client's choice with documented advice.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Dark exposed door → heat build-up → warping → hardware failure → replacement → client complaint and professional liability. Consequence: Black door on north-facing facade without adequate shading → warps within 18 months → hardware no longer aligns → door difficult to operate → replacement demanded → professional indemnity claim.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Solar exposure risk assessed before door specification finalised. Client advised in writing if dark finish specified against recommendation. Concealment point: Once door installed, solar damage is a warranty and liability issue that cannot be undone. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: Manufacturer warranty (not AS) — no specific NCC/AS mapping identified. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.
