Title: Tile and Stone Sample vs Installed Field Appearance
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00072: Tile and Stone Sample vs Installed Field Appearance. Trigger: Small tile or stone sample being approved for use across a much larger installed field.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Tile or stone selection being made. Sample has been provided. Selection rule: A 100mm x 100mm tile sample is not a meaningful representation of a 600mm x 600mm tile in an installed field. The veining or pattern subtle at sample scale can read as dominant at full size. Where a tile has few print variants (7 or 9 unique tiles in a repeating batch), the pattern repeat becomes visible across a large installation — creating what looks like prison bars. For natural stone, no two slabs are the same, and the client must view and approve the actual
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Number of print variants in production run; degree of veining or movement; installed field size; whether natural stone or engineered tile. Alternatives: Approve from showroom sample; inspect multiple full tiles from production run; visit supplier and view assembled boards; for natural stone, view and approve actual slab.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Small sample approved → bulk material installed → pattern repetition reads differently at full scale → expensive aesthetic disappointment. Consequence: 7-variant tile approved from small sample → 80 square metres installed → pattern repeat creates visible horizontal lines every 7 tiles → client finds unacceptable → full tile removal and replacement → $15,000-$25,000 cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Designer and client have viewed full-size tiles or assembled multiple tiles before order. For natural stone, actual slab approved. Pattern repeat assessed. Concealment point: Once tiles installed, pattern repeat problem is obvious and expensive to reverse. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — expert material selection judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Selections Schedule as Builder Handoff Document
L1 Factual Knowledge: Decision captured in CDO-00073: Selections Schedule as Builder Handoff Document. Trigger: Material selections sufficiently resolved — schedule handed to builder for procurement and construction.
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Preconditions: Selections complete or substantially complete. Builder ready to proceed with procurement. Selection rule: Architects and town planners often include indicative colours on documents submitted for council approval — these are placeholders to satisfy the colour requirement, not final selections. The interior designer must replace these with actual specified products. A builder who proceeds to procurement on a schedule containing council-approval placeholder colours will order the wrong product. The handoff document must make absolutely clear
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Conditions and variables: Whether design team includes an architect with placeholder colours in planning documents; whether all selections confirmed; whether builder understands which items are final. Alternatives: Issue schedule including final and indicative colours without distinguishing them; issue clean schedule showing only confirmed selections with unresolved items flagged; issue complete schedule cross-referenced to specification.
L4 Expert Judgement: Failure mode: Placeholder mistaken for final → wrong material/colour procured → variation and rework. Consequence: Architect uses yellow render as planning placeholder → designer does not update schedule → builder orders yellow render → client objects → material may already be ordered → dispute.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Evidence of completion: Schedule clearly distinguishes confirmed final selections from indicative or pending items. Builder briefed on any unconfirmed items. Concealment point: Once procurement proceeds, builder and supplier rely on what is documented. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No NCC/AS mapping — professional documentation and communication judgement. Verification passes A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Hydrostatic Test and OTR Inspection Protocol — Under-Slab Sanitary Drainage — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00007 risk and verification focus: Hydrostatic Test and OTR Inspection Protocol — Under-Slab Sanitary Drainage. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Drain not tested before slab pour; drain not compliant with grade or bedding requirements; inspection not booked; COC not lodged. Consequence chain: Defect concealed under slab → settlement causes low point in drain → blockage and gurgling at floor wastes (first symptom: anti-siphonage failure) → camera investigation required → slab cutting to expose and replace drain section → loss of building use during works → cost: $5,000–$30,000+ depending on extent. Plumber's licence number on COC means 5-year personal liability exposure.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: OTR inspector issues approval (or no-objection notice). COC is lodged. Slab pour can proceed. All documentation retained by the plumber for the 5-year compliance window. Concealment point: Once the slab is poured, the under-slab drainage is permanently concealed. Any defect discovered after the slab is poured requires core-drilling or slab saw-cutting to investigate and rectify — extremely costly. Camera inspection can be used but is expensive and not always conclusive.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Weather forecast (rain can destroy bedding before inspection); site programme and scheduling pressure; proximity of the slab pour date; quality of bedding installation; risk of drain settlement on filled sites. Reversibility: No — once poured, slab cutting is the only access method. Full rework of the affected section required. Very high cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Book the OTR inspection before 3pm on the day prior. Ensure the drain remains completely exposed and unbackfilled — the inspector must see all elements. Place the system under hydrostatic test at 10 kPa minimum for a minimum of 15 minutes before the inspector arrives. Inspector will check: (1) absence of leaks; (2) consistent grade; (3) quality of bedding. Minor defects may be rectified within the inspection window. Major non-compliance requires full rework and rebooking — a significant delay and cost. Do not schedule over a weekend

Title: Under-Slab vs External Sanitary Drain Routing — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00008 risk and verification focus: Under-Slab vs External Sanitary Drain Routing. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: External route attempted on a site where the geometry does not support it — drain cannot maintain minimum cover and required gradient simultaneously. Or under-slab drain installed without adequate bedding or expansion control. Consequence chain: External route failure: drain runs too shallow (< 300 mm) — vulnerable to garden spikes and root intrusion → pipe breakage → sewage in garden. Under-slab failure: inadequate bedding → settlement under slab → cracked pipe → effluent in fill beneath slab → slab heave or structural movement → very expe
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Under-slab route: drain is inspected and hydrostatic tested before slab pour (see CDO-00007). External route: drain is inspected and tested before backfilling. Grade is checked with a level. Concealment point: Under-slab: permanently concealed by the slab once poured. External route: concealed once backfilled and paths/landscaping are installed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Width of available side space; depth of the sewer connection (the deeper the connection, the more fall is available before the drain descends below footing level); footing type and depth; site slope; whether the drain must pass through or under footing beams (requiring lagging); presence of stormwater pipes competing for side-access space. Reversibility: External drain above cover minimum: can be deepened if caught early. Under-slab drain: no — slab cutting required once poured. High cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Check the depth of the sewer connection first — this is the controlling datum. If sufficient external side space exists (typically at least 1.5–2 m given the 300 mm cover requirement and the height-to-length geometry as the drain descends below the footings), an external route is feasible. If the side space is insufficient — as is common on tight urban lots — the under-slab route is the only practical option. Title: Wet Area Substrate Selection — Fibre Cement vs Aquacheck vs Standard Plasterboard — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00027 risk and verification focus: Wet Area Substrate Selection — Fibre Cement vs Aquacheck vs Standard Plasterboard. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Standard plasterboard used in a wet area; or aquacheck used in residential without adequate waterproofing quality assurance. Consequence chain: Incorrect substrate in wet area → waterproofing membrane applied over inadequate base → membrane cracks at flexing joints → water penetrates → substrate saturates → swells and delaminates → tiles de-bond → full tile strip, substrate replacement, re-waterproof, re-tile. Cost: $5,000–$20,000+ depending on area.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Wet area sheets are confirmed as fibre cement (residential) or approved proprietary board (commercial) before installation. Waterproofing contractor has confirmed their system is compatible with the substrate. Concealment point: Once waterproofing membrane and tiles are installed, the substrate is permanently concealed. Any moisture damage to an incorrect substrate will manifest years later as tile movement, grout cracking, and mould.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Building type (residential vs commercial — changes the default selection); waterproofing system quality; tile weight (affects fixing centres — see CDO-00028); whether the substrate will ever be accessible again after tiles are installed. Reversibility: No — once tiled. Full strip-out required to access and replace the substrate.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: For residential: fibre cement is the standard selection. It holds its structural integrity better when wet. For commercial: aquacheck or equivalent proprietary board is standard — easier to cut, handle and work with, but entirely dependent on the quality of the waterproofing membrane over it. If the waterproofing fails, aquacheck degrades rapidly when wetted. The tiler's and waterproofer's quality is therefore the critical dependency for aquacheck installations. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK]. Pass A/

Title: Wet Area Fixing Schedule — Screw Spacing by Tile Weight — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00028 risk and verification focus: Wet Area Fixing Schedule — Screw Spacing by Tile Weight. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Standard 200mm fixing centres used in wet area without checking tile weight. Heavy tiles installed over under-fixed substrate. Consequence chain: Under-fixed substrate flexes under tile load → grout cracks → water ingress → substrate damage → tiles de-bond → full strip-out. Practitioner acknowledged this was common residential practice — a systemic standards gap.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Fixing schedule is confirmed against the tile specification before installation is completed. Where tile weight is unknown, the 100mm schedule (12.5–32kg/m²) is applied as the conservative default. Concealment point: Once waterproofing membrane and tiles are installed, fixing spacing is permanently inaccessible. Deficient fixing only becomes apparent when tiles begin to de-bond.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Tile weight per m² (the governing variable); tile format (large format tiles exert different point loads); whether tiles are a future client choice (common in residential — substrate must be fixed to the heavier category to be safe). Reversibility: No — once tiled. The fixing is concealed and inaccessible without full tile removal.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: The fixing schedule must match the tile weight. In residential practice it is common to use the same fixing centres regardless of tile weight — this is non-compliant. The consequences are a substrate that moves under heavy tile loading, grout cracking, and eventual tile de-bonding. The lining fixer must confirm the tile specification before completing the wet area fixing, because once the waterproofing membrane and tiles are installed, the fixing spacing is permanently concealed. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification

Title: Roof Structural Support for Indoor HVAC Unit — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00047 risk and verification focus: Roof Structural Support for Indoor HVAC Unit. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Unit placed on inadequate framing → persistent dead load on unintended member → deflection or structural failure → difficult rectification. Consequence chain: HVAC unit on undesigned truss member → sustained dead load → truss deflects → ceiling drops → HVAC unit shifts → refrigerant pipe stress or leak → full ceiling and structural remediation.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Truss design or structural design specifically provides for HVAC unit dead load at nominated position. Concealment point: Once unit is installed and ceilings are in, structural deflection is difficult to observe and hard to rectify.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Unit mass and position (must match structural design); whether builder has coordinated with structural engineer; whether truss shop drawings specify an HVAC support. Reversibility: Low after unit installation if structural support was not resolved beforehand.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Modern residential roof trusses are not designed for permanent dead load of an HVAC indoor unit. A person standing briefly on a truss is a live load; a 50-100kg HVAC unit sitting permanently is a dead load the truss was not designed to carry. The builder must ensure the structural engineer or truss manufacturer has designed a specific support location for the unit at the correct position. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 structural performance; AS 4440 roof truss installation]. Pass A/B/C: Not

Title: Temporary Bracing of Erected Wall Frames — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00004 risk and verification focus: Temporary Bracing of Erected Wall Frames. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: No temporary bracing installed after wall erection, or bracing is inadequate for the wind/load conditions. Consequence chain: Unbraced wall frame in wind → frame acts as a sail → frame overturns or racks → potential collapse of frame onto workers below or adjacent → injury or fatality. Even partial racking before collapse: frame geometry distorted → permanent bracing installed to a twisted frame → plumb/square problems carry through to lining and finishes. Immediate risk: High.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Frame is plumb (checked with spirit level or plumb bob) and square (diagonals checked). Bracing is fixed at both face and slab. Certifier framing inspection will check permanent bracing — temporary bracing is removed before this point. Concealment point: Temporary bracing is removed before permanent bracing inspection. There is no long-term concealment risk for temporary bracing itself, but inadequate bracing during the construction phase creates an immediate collapse risk.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Wind exposure at the time of construction (higher wind = more bracing required); presence and location of in-slab services (changes fixing method); height and length of wall frame; temporary loads from workers; time between erection and permanent bracing installation. Reversibility: If the frame is temporarily distorted but not collapsed, it may be correctable before permanent bracing is installed. Once permanent bracing is fixed to a racked frame, the distortion is effectively locked in.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Every wall frame must be temporarily braced immediately after erection and before any person works on or around it. The frame acts like a sail under wind load and is structurally unstable until permanent bracing is complete. Temporary bracing is fixed to the slab — either with masonry nails or masonry anchors. Anchors are preferred where in-slab services are present, as nails driven into a service pipe create a defect that may not be visible for years. Check service locations before drilling. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021 + WHS

Title: Site Induction — Universal Requirement Before Entry — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00010 risk and verification focus: Site Induction — Universal Requirement Before Entry. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Person enters site without induction. Site conditions, plant movements, or hazards differ from their expectation. Person is injured or causes injury to others. Consequence chain: Uninducted person encounters a site-specific hazard → injury → investigation reveals no induction record → builder/PCBU liable for failure to provide site-specific induction → WHS prosecution or civil liability. The absence of an induction record is often the decisive factor in liability determinations.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Induction record is signed by the entrant. Site register shows all current personnel have been inducted. Emergency contact and evacuation point are confirmed understood. Concealment point: There is no concealment point for an induction failure — but the consequence of a person entering without site-specific knowledge is that they act on general assumptions rather than actual current site conditions.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Frequency of visits by the same person (annual induction vs every visit); whether site conditions have changed since the last induction; type of visitor (worker, inspector, owner); current site hazards. Reversibility: Cannot undo an injury. The only corrective measure is to ensure all subsequent entrants are inducted. Civil and regulatory liability follows.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Every person entering the site — regardless of experience, White Card status, trade licence, or number of previous site visits — receives a site-specific induction before entry. Even repeat subcontractors on annual or periodic induction cycles receive an update when site conditions have materially changed. Inspectors, bank representatives, and union officials are not exempt. White Card provides baseline awareness but does not substitute for site-specific knowledge. Standard reference: WHS Act 2012 (SA) s.17; clause verification: Veri

Title: Worker Override Authority — Safety-First Escalation Despite Supervisor — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00011 risk and verification focus: Worker Override Authority — Safety-First Escalation Despite Supervisor. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Worker defers to the supervisor and continues work in the presence of a genuinely serious hazard. Hazard materialises. Consequence chain: Gas leak normalised → accumulation → ignition or health effects → workers injured or fatality → investigation reveals worker raised concern and was overridden → supervisor and PCBU liable → workers' compensation and WHS prosecution.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: The hazard is resolved — either by demonstrating it is genuinely non-critical, or by stopping work and remedying the condition. The resolution is documented in the Take 5 or SWMS. Concealment point: Some hazards — gas accumulation, structural instability — become harder to assess as conditions change. The window for safe intervention may close.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Nature and immediacy of the hazard; relative expertise of the worker and supervisor; programme pressure; whether other workers are at risk; regulatory requirements. Reversibility: Cannot reverse an injury or fatality. The failure to act on a genuine safety concern is one of the most serious findings in a WHS investigation.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Where a worker genuinely believes a hazard presents a serious risk, they have the right and responsibility to escalate that assessment even when the supervisor does not share it. A gas leak that is described as 'only a little bit' is still a gas leak — a small leak can still cause health effects without ignition. The selection rule is: when in doubt, adopt the safer course rather than normalising a seemingly small hazard. The resolution should be on a safety-first basis, not a productivity-first basis. Standard reference: Safe Work A

Title: Plant and Pedestrian Separation — Active Control at Site Interface — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00012 risk and verification focus: Plant and Pedestrian Separation — Active Control at Site Interface. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Plant and pedestrians share a space without active separation. Operator does not see a pedestrian. Collision occurs. Consequence chain: Plant-pedestrian collision → serious injury or fatality → investigation reveals no dedicated spotter, no formal separation → PCBU and site supervisor liable → WHS prosecution, civil liability, reputational damage.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: The operating zone is clear of non-essential personnel. A spotter is in position before plant moves to or across the site boundary. No pedestrian-plant conflict occurs. Concealment point: Plant movements on site create an immediate risk that is not concealed — but the consequences of a collision are severe and irreversible.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Type of plant (bobcat vs semi-trailer); proximity to public footpath; pedestrian volume; site boundary position; council permissions; visibility conditions. Reversibility: Cannot reverse a plant-pedestrian collision. The consequences — serious injury, fatality — are permanent.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: During plant clearing, excavation or material delivery, no non-essential person is in the operating zone. This is non-negotiable — rely on exclusion, not operator awareness. Where plant must cross a public footpath, a dedicated second person controls the sequence — pedestrians stop before plant moves, or plant stops for pedestrians. Simultaneous crossing is never permitted. Formal pedestrian diversion requires council permission; a gate/spotter manages the interface where formal diversion is not granted. Standard reference: AS/NZS 30

Title: Hazardous Discovery During Excavation — Stop Work and Specialist Response — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00013 risk and verification focus: Hazardous Discovery During Excavation — Stop Work and Specialist Response. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Excavation continues after hazardous material is struck. Material is fragmented and dispersed. Workers are exposed to fibres or contaminants. Consequence chain: Asbestos pipe struck and fragmented → fibres released → workers and neighbours exposed → stop-work order from EPA → specialist remediation required → civil liability for exposure → regulatory prosecution. Old-farm sites with buried asbestos cement pipe are a specific risk on greenfield SA residential sites.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Work is stopped. A cordon is established. The specialist or authority is notified. No further disturbance occurs until the material is assessed. Documentation of the discovery, response, and clearance is retained. Concealment point: Once hazardous material is disturbed — particularly asbestos — fibres are released and cannot be recalled. Further disturbance dramatically increases exposure risk and remediation cost.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Site history and likely materials; type and condition of the material; whether further disturbance has occurred before the hazard was recognised; regulatory requirements for the specific material type. Reversibility: Cannot reverse exposure once it has occurred. Remediation is costly. Legal liability for asbestos exposure is long-tail.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Stop work immediately when an unexpected material is encountered and its hazard level cannot be confirmed from visual inspection. Do not attempt to establish the extent of the material by further excavation. Where asbestos is confirmed or suspected, notify the EPA and engage a licensed asbestos removalist before any further disturbance. Where the material is non-hazardous (confirmed by specialist), the company may organise removal internally. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3:2018; clause verification: Verified. Pass A/B/C: Not Start

Title: Hot Work Near Combustibles — Fire Control and Trade Coordination — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00015 risk and verification focus: Hot Work Near Combustibles — Fire Control and Trade Coordination. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Hot work proceeds while other trades are using combustible coatings or materials in the same space. Ignition occurs. Consequence chain: Plumber soldering near painter using solvent-based undercoat → paint ignites → fire spreads → damage to structure, tools, materials → possible injury → investigation reveals concurrent trades in the same space → site supervisor liable for failure to coordinate hot work with combustible operations.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Fire extinguishers are confirmed present and appropriate before hot work begins. No other trades with combustible materials are working in the immediate zone. Fire watch is maintained. No ignition occurs. Concealment point: Once combustible material ignites, the window for effective intervention is very short — particularly in enclosed or partially enclosed buildings.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Type of hot work; type of combustible material; enclosure/ventilation; proximity of other trades; weather/wind conditions. Reversibility: A small fire can be extinguished if the right equipment is immediately available. A large fire is not recoverable. The sequence of events is very fast once ignition occurs.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Before any hot work begins, confirm: (1) appropriate fire extinguishers are present on site — both water (for timber/materials) and dry chemical (for flammable liquids/electrical); (2) other trades are not working simultaneously with combustible materials in the same space; (3) a fire watch is maintained during and immediately after hot work. A painter applying solvent-based coatings and a plumber soldering in the same space at the same time is not acceptable — this combination caused an actual fire. Standard reference: AS/NZS 3500.3

Title: Electrical Isolation and Tag-Off Before Live Circuit Work — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00016 risk and verification focus: Electrical Isolation and Tag-Off Before Live Circuit Work. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Tag-off is not applied or is removed by a person other than the one who applied it. A circuit is energised while another person is working on or near it. Consequence chain: Energised circuit → electrocution or arc flash → serious injury or fatality → investigation reveals no tag applied or tag removed by wrong person → licensed electrician and PCBU liable → WHS prosecution → potential manslaughter charge if gross negligence is found.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Tag is visibly applied to the isolation point. No circuit is energised without the knowledge and consent of the person who applied the tag. Electrical work is completed and signed off before any related trade is allowed to proceed in the same space. Concealment point: Once a circuit is live, its hazard is invisible — energised conductors look identical to de-energised ones. The concealment is inherent in the nature of electricity.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Stage of electrical installation (rough-in vs final fix vs connected); number and variety of trades in the space; programme pressure; whether the meter has been connected by the network provider. Reversibility: Electrocution injuries range from burn to cardiac arrest to fatality. Burns may require years of treatment. Fatality is irreversible.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Before any trade works on or near an electrical circuit — and before any meter or connection is made live — the circuit must be confirmed isolated and tagged off. A tag is a physical and visible lock that prevents the circuit from being energised by another person. The painter who turned the power on while the electrician was working illustrates the consequence: a tag prevents this because the switch physically cannot be operated without removing the tag. No person other than the person who applied the tag removes it. Standard refere

Title: Overflow Provision — Deliberate Design for Extreme Rainfall — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00018 risk and verification focus: Overflow Provision — Deliberate Design for Extreme Rainfall. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: No deliberate overflow path provided. Extreme rainfall event exceeds gutter capacity. Water overflows into the building rather than away from it. Consequence chain: No overflow provision → extreme rainfall → water backs up behind fascia or flows into roof space → ceiling damage, mould, structural damage to top plates → warranty claim → investigation finds no overflow provision → builder and roof plumber liable.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: The overflow path is traceable from the design drawings. Where a controlled back overflow is used, the gutter is set off the fascia at the correct distance. Where a rainhead is used, the overflow geometry is unobstructed. The overflow discharges to a location that does not damage the building or neighbouring property. Concealment point: Once the roof and cladding are complete, the overflow arrangement is concealed or inaccessible. Failure is only discovered during a significant rainfall event.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Gutter profile (determines what overflow methods are available); building form (parapet, box gutter, balcony — each requires different treatment); architectural covers/shrouds on rainheads; proximity of the overflow path to habitable areas or neighbouring property. Reversibility: Retrofitting an overflow path after installation typically requires gutter removal and refixing. High cost and disruption.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: A deliberate overflow path must be provided as part of the gutter design — not as an optional extra. Freeboard provides some buffer, but the standard requires overflow to be managed, not merely tolerated. For standard domestic gutters (D or OG profile), a controlled back overflow arrangement is a common acceptable method. For box gutters, a dedicated overflow slot or rainhead is required. Title: Non-Compliant Design — Installer's Obligation to Escalate Before Installation — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00024 risk and verification focus: Non-Compliant Design — Installer's Obligation to Escalate Before Installation. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Installer proceeds with a known non-compliant detail without raising a formal objection. Heavy rainfall events expose the performance failure. Multiple dwellings in a repeat-build subdivision affected. Consequence chain: Non-compliant roof drainage → heavy rainfall event → flooding of dwellings → investigation identifies the pitch/valley non-compliance → all parties in the design-construction chain examined → installer who completed the work without objecting faces liability even though the non-compliance originated upstream.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Non-compliance is identified before installation. Written notice is provided to the builder. The detail is corrected or an alternative is agreed before installation proceeds. If the builder directs the installer to proceed despite the written concern, that instruction and the installer's objection are both documented. Concealment point: Once installed and subsequent work proceeds (sarking, ceilings, cladding), the non-compliant detail is concealed. The failure is only discovered when a heavy rainfall event exposes the performance gap.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Nature of the non-compliance; certainty of the installer's assessment; consequences of the non-compliance in heavy rainfall; financial and programme pressure to proceed; whether the work is part of a repeat/volume-build where the same error will be replicated. Reversibility: Remediating a non-compliant roof drainage system after completion requires removing and replacing roof sheeting, valleys, and gutters. For a whole subdivision, the cost is catastrophic.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: The worst outcome is completing a known non-compliant installation. The installer is not excused by the fact that the designer, builder, or certifier has approved or repeated the detail — each party has their own responsibility at their decision point. Where a non-compliance is identified: stop before installing the affected element; contact the builder in writing describing the concern; do not proceed until the detail is confirmed compliant or changed. Compliance limits are not negotiated away for financial pressure or programme urg

Title: Expansion Joint Placement — Ceilings Exceeding 12 Metres — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00029 risk and verification focus: Expansion Joint Placement — Ceilings Exceeding 12 Metres. Safety severity: Low; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: No expansion joint installed in a ceiling run exceeding 12m; or joint placed at wrong location. Consequence chain: Building movement → ceiling lining cracks at the point of highest stress (typically at the external wall junction or mid-span of the long run) → crack visible through paint → investigation reveals no expansion joint → strip affected section, install joint, re-sheet, re-flush, re-paint.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Ceiling plan is reviewed before sheeting begins. All runs exceeding 12m are identified and expansion joint locations are marked. Joint is installed as sheeting proceeds — it cannot be retrofitted. Concealment point: Once the ceiling is flushed and painted, the absence of an expansion joint is invisible until the ceiling cracks at the location where a joint should have been.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Total ceiling run (the threshold is 12m); frame type (steel vs timber — changes urgency); whether the building is in a climate with significant temperature range; whether the open plan area crosses a structural zone boundary. Reversibility: Cannot be retrofitted without stripping. Highly disruptive after ceiling is finished.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Any ceiling run exceeding 12 metres in a single direction requires an expansion joint to accommodate movement of the building structure relative to the lining. The threshold is 12 metres. Joints are typically placed between external wall zones where differential movement is likely. Steel-framed buildings require more careful attention to this requirement than timber-framed buildings because steel expands and contracts more significantly with temperature change. Title: Trade Exclusion During Linings — Silica Dust and Sequencing — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00032 risk and verification focus: Trade Exclusion During Linings — Silica Dust and Sequencing. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Another trade works in the same space during sanding — silica dust exposure occurs without respiratory protection. Consequence chain: Silica exposure → cumulative lung damage → silicosis (irreversible) → WorkCover claim → investigation reveals inadequate site management of silica hazard → builder and lining fixer liable for failure to control the exposure.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: No other trade is present in areas where cutting, sanding, or flushing is active. If a trade arrives unscheduled, they are directed to wait by the site supervisor. Silica controls are in place (respiratory protection, dust suppression or extraction) wherever cutting or sanding occurs. Concealment point: Silica dust is invisible and has no immediate warning symptoms. Cumulative exposure causes silicosis — irreversible and progressive. The concealment is physiological, not physical.

Title: Pre-Slab Electrical Provisions — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00036 risk and verification focus: Pre-Slab Electrical Provisions. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).

Once concrete is placed, any destination requiring a conduit through the slab cannot be served without chasing, demolition, or visible surface routing. A 32mm orange PVC swept-bend conduit costs almost nothing to install before the pour and creates optionality for the building life. It must be secured to reinforcement, raised clear of slab to be visible, and photographed before pour. Title: Pre-Lining Evidence Capture — Photographing Electrical Rough-In — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00041 risk and verification focus: Pre-Lining Evidence Capture — Photographing Electrical Rough-In. Safety severity: Low; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: No photographic record → later trade penetrates cable → dispute → no evidence → cost borne by electrician. Consequence chain: Cabinetmaker fixes vanity → drill strikes live cable → builder claims cable was not where electrician said → no photos → dispute → WorkCover investigation.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: All rooms photographed before lining. Photos retained in project file. Builder notified lining can proceed. Concealment point: Lining installation — once lining is fixed, all cable routes are permanently concealed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Upcoming lining programme; complexity of rough-in; number of slab conduits; builder relationship. Reversibility: Not possible to reconstruct after lining without opening walls.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Photographs of the rough-in are the electrician's record of where every cable, conduit, and penetration is located. They serve three purposes: protect the electrician if a future trade penetrates a cable; guide the second-fix technician to exact outlet locations; demonstrate to the certifier that the installation was completed correctly before concealment. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: No specific AS mapping — accepted practice and risk management. Pass A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Electrical Point Survival Through Lining and Tiling Handoff — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00042 risk and verification focus: Electrical Point Survival Through Lining and Tiling Handoff. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Box buried by tiling → second-fix cannot access → tiles removed → retile → delay and variation. Consequence chain: Tiler tiles over electrical box in wet area → box 15mm below tile surface → second-fix cannot install fitting → tiles must be removed → retile.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: All boxes at correct setout for finished surface before tiling. Tiler briefed on box locations. Boxes inspected after tiling before second fix. Concealment point: Once tiles are grouted, electrical box positions are fixed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Tile thickness and type; box setout from rough wall; tiler's awareness of electrical box locations. Reversibility: Low once tiles are grouted.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: The lining and tiling handoff is a common source of electrical damage. A box set slightly too deep when a tile goes over it becomes inaccessible. The electrician should coordinate with the lining fixer and tiler, ensure boxes are at correct setout for finished surface (accounting for tile thickness), and inspect after tiling. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 box setout and accessibility requirements]. Pass A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Energisation Readiness — Final Checks Before Connecting to Supply — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00043 risk and verification focus: Energisation Readiness — Final Checks Before Connecting to Supply. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Premature energisation → concealed wiring fault → electrical fault under load → fire or shock → investigation → no certificate → criminal liability. Consequence chain: Energisation without testing → insulation failure → fire → investigation reveals no test certificate → criminal charges and personal liability.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: All tests completed and results recorded. Certificate of Electrical Compliance prepared. Builder notified energisation can proceed. Concealment point: The installation is live. Faults present at testing but missed may cause injury or fire.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Completeness of second-fix; RCD test results; insulation resistance outcomes; certifier inspection date. Reversibility: Can be de-energised and tested after the fact, but harm caused during the period cannot be undone.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: The electrical installation must be tested and certified before energisation — a legal requirement under AS/NZS 3000 and SA electrical licensing. Testing includes insulation resistance of every circuit, earthing continuity, RCD tripping time and current, and polarity. Every result must be documented. The Certificate of Electrical Compliance must be provided to the customer before use. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 testing and certification; SA Electrical Products Act]. Pass A/B/C: Not St

Title: Failed Electrical Test — Fault Finding Before Certification — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00044 risk and verification focus: Failed Electrical Test — Fault Finding Before Certification. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Unresolved fault certified → energisation → fault manifests → fire or shock → investigation → criminal and civil liability. Consequence chain: Failed insulation resistance test → electrician proceeds → cable fault causes fire → investigation reveals test failure was known → criminal charges and full remediation liability.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Fault located and rectified. All tests re-run and pass. Certificate issued. Fault cause documented. Concealment point: None — a failed test resolved before certification has no downstream consequence.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Fault type; circuit location; accessibility of suspect section; whether lining has been applied. Reversibility: The fault can be found and repaired at any time before energisation. Harm caused cannot be undone.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: A failed test result is diagnostic information, not a reason to certify and hope. Isolate the failed circuit, disconnect loads progressively to locate the fault section, identify the specific cause. Common causes: cable nicked during first-fix; moisture in a wet area box; incorrect termination; damaged insulation at framing penetration. Certifying with a known fault is professional and legal negligence. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 testing and remediation; SA Electrical Products Act]. L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00050 risk and verification focus: Refrigerant Pipework Route and Joint Location. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).

Consequence chain: Joint in inaccessible roof corner develops leak → system loses charge → ceiling must be opened → joint repaired → ceiling patched → significant cost.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Pipe route confirmed before installation. Necessary joints at accessible locations. Insulation and vapour seal complete. Concealment point: Once wall linings and ceilings installed, pipe routes and joints concealed.

L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Joints in refrigerant pipework must be accessible for maintenance. A braze joint concealed in an inaccessible roof corner creates permanent maintenance liability. The route should be planned so any necessary joint is at an accessible location. Running through wall cavity in a new build is strongly preferred. Insulation and vapour seal on suction line is critical — vermin eat insulation, and the exposed suction line runs near dew point. Title: Pre-Commissioning Integrity Gate — Nitrogen Test and Vacuum — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00051 risk and verification focus: Pre-Commissioning Integrity Gate — Nitrogen Test and Vacuum. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Leak or moisture left in system → refrigerant admitted → poor performance, blockage, or release → callback and repair. Consequence chain: System commissioned without vacuum → residual moisture → reacts with refrigerant oil → acid forms in compressor → compressor fails at 2 years → full system replacement.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Nitrogen test passes 24-hour hold. Vacuum achieves and holds below 500 microns. Refrigerant valves opened only after vacuum confirmed. Concealment point: The refrigerant circuit is opened and the system commissioned.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Refrigerant type (changes test pressure); duration of nitrogen hold; whether vacuum holds at target. Reversibility: Rectifiable before commissioning; potentially difficult where leak is concealed.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Pre-commissioning sequence is non-negotiable: nitrogen pressure test first (dry nitrogen, not compressed air which contains moisture), hold 24 hours, then evacuate to below 500 microns (aim for 100 microns or better). Nitrogen is used because it is dry — compressed air contains moisture that reacts with refrigerant or freezes at the expansion device. The system must not be commissioned until the vacuum target is achieved and holds. An experienced technician aims well below 500 microns. Standard reference: not specified; clause verifi

Title: Authorisation and Supervision for Refrigerant and HVAC Work — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00054 risk and verification focus: Authorisation and Supervision for Refrigerant and HVAC Work. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Unlicensed refrigerant handling → WorkSafe investigation → licence suspension → cost and penalty. Consequence chain: Apprentice connects refrigerant lines unsupervised → error → refrigerant release → client property damage → investigation → company loses ARCtick licence → business cannot perform HVAC work.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: All refrigerant-live tasks performed by or under direct supervision of ARCtick-licensed technician. Concealment point: None — correct authorisation prevents liability.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Apprentice stage and training; task type (refrigerant-live vs non-live); availability of licensed technician; client urgency. Reversibility: Licence revocation is not reversible in the short term.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Refrigerant handling in Australia requires an ARCtick licence. An apprentice may perform HVAC work under supervision, but the licensed technician must be present and able to intervene for any task involving live refrigerant. Vacuum and pressure testing, connection of refrigerant lines, and commissioning are not tasks an apprentice should perform unsupervised. Title: Condensate Drain Discharge Location — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00058 risk and verification focus: Condensate Drain Discharge Location. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Inadequate condensate drain → overflow → water damage to ceiling and wall → ceiling must be opened. Consequence chain: Condensate drain connects to blocked external pipe → overflow at indoor unit → water drips onto ceiling lining → ceiling stains and damage → ceiling opened → drain rectified → ceiling replaced.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Condensate drain route confirmed before ceiling closure. Discharge point does not create water damage risk. Drain is insulated where required. Concealment point: Once ceiling is closed, condensate drain is concealed and access is limited.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Indoor unit height relative to drain connections; condensate volume; whether pump is required. Reversibility: Low after ceiling closure.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: A ducted indoor HVAC unit in cooling mode can produce 10-20 litres of condensate per day. This must drain to a point that does not cause water damage or nuisance. Ideal discharge is to plumbing drain. Where gravity is not available, a condensate pump is required. Discharge to outside is acceptable where it does not create ponding, ice, or water damage risk. Condensate drain must be insulated where it passes through warm areas to prevent condensation on the outside of the drain pipe. Standard reference: not specified; clause verificat

Title: HVAC Work Stoppage — When Conditions Are Unsafe — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00059 risk and verification focus: HVAC Work Stoppage — When Conditions Are Unsafe. Safety severity: High; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Continuing work with known hazard → incident → injury → investigation → penalty. Consequence chain: Technician identifies live conductors in roof space → continues work → contacts conductor → electrocution → death → criminal prosecution for failure to provide safe working conditions.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Hazard identified. Work stops. Hazard communicated to responsible party. Work recommences only when hazard is controlled. Concealment point: None — stopping work for safety is always correct.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Type and immediacy of hazard; whether controls can be implemented; supervision available; contractor WHS policy. Reversibility: An injury cannot be undone.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: The HVAC trade involves a uniquely broad range of hazards: high-voltage electrical work; high-pressure refrigerant; working in hot confined roof spaces; chemical exposure; working at height. The default should be to stop when in doubt. The right escalation path is to the builder for site hazards, to the licensed electrician for electrical isolation questions, and to WorkSafe SA for hazards that cannot be resolved through the normal chain of command. source_content.l4: Conditions affecting this decision: Type and immediacy of hazard; whether controls can be implemented; supervision available; contractor WHS policy. Reversibility: An injury cannot be undone.
source_content.l5: Underlying decision: The HVAC trade involves a uniquely broad range of hazards: high-voltage electrical work; high-pressure refrigerant; working in hot confined roof spaces; chemical exposure; working at height. Title: Bathroom Fixture and Layout Change Window — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00060 risk and verification focus: Bathroom Fixture and Layout Change Window. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Late fixture change → existing waste or cavity no longer suits → redesign or invasive plumbing/framing alteration → cost and delay. Consequence chain: Client changes from back-to-wall to wall-hung after first-fix → waste position incompatible → framing modified → plumber relocates waste → retile floor → significant cost and delay.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Fixture type confirmed before first-fix waste positions are established. Concealment point: Once slab and first-fix waste penetrations complete, fixture type changes constrained by existing waste position.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Stage of plumbing first-fix; wall cavity state; client's timeline for decision. Reversibility: High before first fix; very low after slab and first-fix penetrations built.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: A seemingly simple aesthetic change — replacing a back-to-wall toilet with a wall-hung model — has direct structural and plumbing consequences. The wall-hung cistern requires a cavity with specific depth (minimum 150mm rather than 100mm), structural noggins or a dedicated mounting frame, and a tiled access panel. Once the waste penetration is installed and the frame is built, changing the toilet type is not a minor adjustment. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 sanitary plumbing; AS/NZS 3500.2 f

Title: Tile Size and Layout Selection for Wet Areas — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00061 risk and verification focus: Tile Size and Layout Selection for Wet Areas. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Inappropriate tile size/set-out → awkward cuts or inability to achieve falls → poor drainage or appearance → strip-out required. Consequence chain: Large format tiles selected → floor fall cannot be achieved without significant cutting → tiler advises cannot achieve even fall → strip drain specified → floor screed modified → delay and variation.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Tile size, bond, and set-out confirmed before waterproofing. Set-out drawing shows cut tile sizes at all terminations. Concealment point: Once waterproofing and screed installed, floor fall is fixed. Once tiles installed, set-out is fixed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Floor fall requirements; room width and length; ceiling height; bath or shower position. Reversibility: High before tile order; very low after waterproofing and tiling.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Tile size and floor falls interact directly — a very large format tile (600x1200) is difficult to cut to achieve required fall without large visible obviously non-level pieces. The room dimensions determine how many full tiles can be achieved before a cut. The set-out should be worked back from the most visually prominent fixed element (bath face, entry, shower head wall) rather than from a corner. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — NCC 2022 Vol 2 wet area; AS 3740 waterproofing; AS/NZS 4671 floor falls]

Title: Roof Geometry Set-Out Sequence — Mark Roof Before Erecting Walls — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00002 risk and verification focus: Roof Geometry Set-Out Sequence — Mark Roof Before Erecting Walls. Safety severity: Low; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Roof set-out done from a ladder after erection — increased error rate, safety risk, and time cost. Or studs positioned first without regard to roof load paths. Consequence chain: Error in set-out → rafter positions misaligned with studs → load path discontinuity → double top plate or blocking required as a corrective measure (adds cost and time) → OR roof geometry errors require truss/rafter relocation before lining. Safety risk: working at height to correct what could have been done safely at ground level.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Roof set-out marks are visible on the top plate. Rafter/truss positions align with stud positions below, confirming load path continuity. Certifier framing inspection. Concealment point: Roof geometry is effectively locked in once rafters/trusses are installed and the roof frame is permanent-braced. No opportunity to revise the geometry after this point without significant rework.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Roof type (hip, gable, skillion — changes the set-out geometry); roof sheet type (1200 mm vs 900 mm rafter/purlin centres for sheet metal); building span; architect specification of rafter spacing; number of storeys. Reversibility: Partially — a double top plate or blocking can correct a load-path misalignment, but this adds material cost and is not ideal. Roof geometry errors are very costly to correct after trusses are fixed.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Mark the roof set-out (jack rafter position, half-span, first common rafter centre) on the wall plates while they are flat on the ground. This is significantly safer and more accurate than doing the same work from a ladder after the frame is erected. The set-out also determines where studs must be positioned to maintain the continuous load path from roof to slab. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021; clause verification: [CHECK]. Pass A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.

Title: Double Top Plate or Blocking — When Load Path Continuity Requires It — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00003 risk and verification focus: Double Top Plate or Blocking — When Load Path Continuity Requires It. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Load path discontinuity not addressed — no double plate or blocking installed where required. Consequence chain: Concentrated roof load applied to top plate at a point with no stud below → top plate deflection over time → ceiling and wall cracking → in severe cases, structural movement visible in frame → engineer assessment required → costly remediation involving lining removal and structural intervention.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Visual inspection: the double plate or blocking is visible during the framing inspection. Certifier framing hold point confirms load path is continuous before lining. Concealment point: Once lining is fixed, the load transfer arrangement is permanently concealed. No access without strip-out.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Degree of misalignment between rafter/truss and stud (small misalignment may be acceptable under AS 1684.2; larger requires intervention); whether trusses or cut rafters are used (trusses are manufactured to a layout that may not align with studs); presence of girder trusses (concentrated loads at specific points); wall height and span. Reversibility: No — once lining is on and structure is loaded, correction requires lining removal and significant framing intervention. Cost: high.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Where a roof member loads the top plate at a point that does not bear directly over a stud, a double top plate or blocking must be provided to distribute that load to the nearest stud. The double plate acts as a transfer element. Blocking is an alternative where space permits. The preferred approach — identified by the practitioner — is to mark roof positions before setting stud layout so that load paths can be aligned from the outset, eliminating the need for this corrective measure. Standard reference: AS 1684.2:2021; clause verifi

Title: Roof Catchment Sizing — ARI Selection and Effective Area Calculation — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00017 risk and verification focus: Roof Catchment Sizing — ARI Selection and Effective Area Calculation. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Drainage system sized below the design event. Gutters overflow in a significant rainfall. Water enters the building or causes damage. Consequence chain: Under-sized gutter overflows in a design event → water runs behind cladding or through ceiling penetrations → ceiling damage, mould, structural damage → warranty claim → investigation finds drainage was under-sized relative to the applicable ARI → roof plumber liable for design/sizing failure. Climate-change note: design events may occur more frequently than the ARI interval implies.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Calculation is documented and matches the installed gutter, downpipe, and overflow configuration. Where software is used, manual cross-check of one zone is retained as evidence of verification. Concealment point: Once gutters, downpipes, and roof sheets are installed and ceilings are lined, the drainage system is effectively locked in. No visible indication of under-sizing until a significant rainfall event.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Geographic location (changes ARI intensity); roof pitch (changes effective catchment area); roof type and profile (changes available gutter/downpipe options); building form (broken hips, valleys, porticos increase complexity); design event (20-year ARI for domestic, other for commercial). Reversibility: Once installed and the roof and ceiling are complete, resizing requires removing gutters and potentially the roof sheeting. High cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Identify the project location and look up the 20-year ARI rainfall intensity for that location. Convert the 2D plan area to effective sloping catchment area using the pitch multiplier. Divide the roof into drainage zones, each with one or more downpipes. For each zone, calculate the peak flow rate in litres per second and confirm that the selected gutter profile and downpipe diameter can pass that flow. Where software is used, verify that the inputs and output make sense before accepting the result. Standard reference: WHS Act 2012 (

Title: Valley Sheet Fixing — Thermal Movement Allowance — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00020 risk and verification focus: Valley Sheet Fixing — Thermal Movement Allowance. Safety severity: Low; concealment risk: Yes; downstream reach: Medium (2-3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Valley sheet screw-fixed in a restraining manner. Sheet expands and contracts with temperature changes. Sheet tears around fixings over several seasons. Consequence chain: Fixing failure → hole in valley sheet → water enters roof space → ceiling damage, mould, potential structural damage → warranty claim or defect liability → concealed by overlapping sheets, difficult to diagnose without destructive investigation.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Fixing method is consistent with the applicable standard or manufacturer requirement. No rigid fixings restrain thermal movement along the length of the sheet. Concealment point: Valley sheets are concealed by the overlapping roof sheets from above. Once installed, the fixing method is not visible. Failure (tearing around fixings) appears as a water leak, often years after installation.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Material type (different metals have different thermal expansion coefficients); valley length (longer valleys experience greater total movement); local temperature range; roof orientation and shading. Reversibility: Once the roof sheets are fixed over the valley, replacing the valley sheet is invasive — surrounding sheets must be removed. High cost.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Valley sheets are flat — unlike corrugated roof sheeting, they have no profile geometry to absorb thermal movement. On a hot day, a flat metal valley sheet will expand along its length. If it is screw-fixed in a way that restrains that movement, the sheet will tear around the fixing over time. The correct fixing method allows the sheet to slide while remaining weather-sealed. Direct screw fixing into the valley is a common but non-compliant practice. Title: Downpipe and Stormwater Drainage Coordination — Trade Interface Decision — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00022 risk and verification focus: Downpipe and Stormwater Drainage Coordination — Trade Interface Decision. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: No coordination occurs. Roofing completes with downpipes in positions that do not align with stormwater infrastructure. Unsightly bends or serious misalignment at the connection. Consequence chain: Misaligned connection → additional bends reduce hydraulic performance → partial blockage risk → water diverted in extreme rainfall → pooling near the foundation → reactive soil movement → structural damage to the slab. Alternatively: stormwater not connected at all → water discharging to the surface → neighbour and erosion complaints → council en
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Downpipe positions are agreed before either system is installed. The stormwater plan shows invert locations that align with the roof drainage design. No visible offsets or bends are required at the downpipe-to-stormwater junction. Concealment point: Once the roof is sheeted and the slab/paths are poured, the junction between downpipe and stormwater is physically fixed. Correction requires opening up the ground connection.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Site geometry and available fall; reactive soil risk (increases consequence of poor stormwater); contract scope and trade procurement sequence; whether the builder coordinates trades directly or each trade procures separately. Reversibility: After installation, repositioning either the downpipe or the stormwater connection requires opening the ground connection, patching surfaces, and recoating. High disruption.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Coordinate downpipe positions and stormwater invert locations before either system is installed. The builder owns this coordination — it is not the responsibility of either plumbing trade to discover the other's work on site. Failure to coordinate results in misalignment, visible bends, and additional fittings that look unprofessional and reduce hydraulic performance. Stormwater should be planned early — not deferred to project close-out — because it is one of the most consequential systems in the building in terms of structural prot

Title: Internal Linings Pre-Start Conditions — Weatherproofing and Trade Readiness — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00025 risk and verification focus: Internal Linings Pre-Start Conditions — Weatherproofing and Trade Readiness. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Commencement despite moisture or inadequate weatherproofing — plasterboard absorbs moisture, swells, loses structural integrity, and delaminates from fixings. Consequence chain: Moisture-affected sheets installed → swelling causes surface irregularity → delamination and nail pops within weeks → full strip-out and re-sheet required → dispute with builder about who bears the cost → lining fixer's reputation and contractor relationship damaged.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: Visual inspection on site confirms roof is complete and weathertight. Sarking or cladding is in place on all external walls. No moisture visible on slab or frame. Sheet storage area (garage) is dry. Concealment point: Once lining is installed and moisture is trapped behind it, the damage is not visible until mould appears or the sheets delaminate — which may be months later.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Season (winter vs summer — changes acceptable weatherproofing standard); moisture inside the frame; builder time pressure (a common source of pressure to commence early); stage of other trades. Reversibility: Once sheets are taped, flushed, and painted, moisture damage is concealed until it manifests as visible defects. At that point strip-out is the only remedy.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: Three preconditions must be confirmed before commencing. First: the roof must be on — no exceptions regardless of builder assurance about timing. Second: external cladding or at minimum sarking wrap must be in place. In summer, wrap-only may be acceptable if no moisture is present; in winter or wet conditions, wrap-only is insufficient and full cladding is preferred. Title: Wet Area Electrical Location Verification After Fixture Changes — risk, evidence and verification
L1 Factual Knowledge: CDO-00034 risk and verification focus: Wet Area Electrical Location Verification After Fixture Changes. Safety severity: Medium; concealment risk: No; downstream reach: High (>3).
L2 Procedural Knowledge: Failure mode: Fixture moved after rough-in → electrical point non-compliant → late relocation → finish disruption and variation. Consequence chain: Fixture moves → electrical point in exclusion zone → certifier identifies non-compliance → tiles opened → cable relocated → retile → cost exceeds cost of early re-check.
L3 Conditional Knowledge: Evidence required: All electrical locations re-checked against actual post-change fixture positions before second fix. Concealment point: Once wet-area tiles are installed, fixture positions and electrical locations are permanently committed.
L4 Expert Judgement: Conditions affecting this decision: Post-rough-in fixture change; proximity to exclusion zone; zone classification (Zone 0, 1, 2); equipment type available. Reversibility: Moderate before finishes; low once wet-area finishes committed.
L5 Context and Dependencies: Underlying decision: A minor plumbing or design change can invalidate an electrical location. The 500mm zone from a sink or bath is a compliance threshold — 505mm complies, 495mm does not. Any fixture movement must trigger re-check of every electrical location in that wet area against AS/NZS 3000 exclusion zone requirements. Standard reference: not specified; clause verification: [CHECK — AS/NZS 3000 wet-area Zones 0, 1, 2]. Pass A/B/C: Not Started/Not Started/Not Started.
